speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Acting Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: TABLING OP ORDER IN COUNCIL-STATEMENT ON ORGANIZATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I beg leave to lay on the table an order in council which establishes the Canadian information service. This service is being set up to provide for the distribution of information about Canada to the peoples of other countries.
Canadian Information Service

The need for such a service has been generally recognized. Canada has a vital interest in international peace and prosperity, and an important part to play in the attainment of these objectives. It is essential, therefore, that our people and country be known and understood abroad.
Those with whom we trade must know our country and its possibilities; those with whom we are associated for the maintenance of world security must know with whom they are cooperating, and what may be expected of our cooperation. In short, both trade and diplomacy, to be carried out successfully, need a background of understanding based on factual information objectively presented.
During the war years Canada's diplomatic representation abroad has had to be increased to keep pace with our increased obligations. In 1939 we maintained only four missions; to-day we have high commissioners in all the capitals of the commonwealth, and ambassadors and ministers in many other countries. At the same time the network of trade commissioners is being increased with a view to giving the utmost help to Canadian trade, which means, in the last analysis, help to every Canadian. All these representatives need to be kept thoroughly informed about what is going on at home.
During the last three years, pioneer work in the way of supplying information abroad has been done through the wartime information board, in conjunction with embassies, legations and trade commissioners. It will be the first duty of the new service to develop adequate reference and information services for all these Canadian representatives abroad. For this reason it was considered advisable to retain an interdepartmental, rather than a purely departmental, service.
The service is to be directed by a committee on which departments and agencies primarily interested in external peace-time information are represented. This committee will be under the chairmanship of A. D. P. Heeney, deputy head of the Privy Council office. It will also include Norman Robertson, Under-Secretary of State for External Affairs; M. W. Mackenzie, Deputy Minister of Trade and Commerce; Doctor Augustin Frigon, general manager of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation; the government film commissioner, and the director of the Canadian information service.
Geoffrey C. Andrew, who has been secretary of the wartime information board for more than two years, and more recently has been acting as general manager, has been appointed director of the new service.

I should like to pay a word of tribute to the work which the wartime information board, and before it the director of public information, performed during the war years. The establishment of an information agency was a relatively new venture for Canada. It was a necessary task, and a difficult one, and much useful work has been done. Since V-J day the board has been steadily cutting down its services within Canada. A few days ago the last general manager of the wartime information board, Mr. A. D. Dunton, returned to his peace-time employment as editor of the Montreal Standard. I think it proper to say that he takes with him the thanks and admiration of all Canadians who can recognize a good and difficult job well done.

speechtext:
I desire to announce to the house that a basis of settlement has been agreed upon with the province of Saskatchewan in reference to the seed grain dispute, so-called, which has been going on between that province and the dominion government. Under this settlement the balance owing the dominion by the province of Saskatchewan in respect of the 193S seed grain loan will be paid by the province as follows:
$6,626,664.68 to be paid monthly as collected from municipalities and to be paid in full as an obligation of the province by July 31, 1948.
$7,570,123.72 to be paid by the province over a period of eleven years.
Pursuant to this settlement the province will undertake to collect in the immediate future the amount owing by the farmer debtors under the compromise which the province made with them last year. As such moneys are collected from the farmers they will be paid by the province to the dominion. The balance of the total outstanding indebtedness will be paid by the province to the dominion, as I have said, over a period of eleven years and will be secured by noninterest bearing treasury bills of the province.
I may add that a statement substantially to this effect was given to the press last night, but it was reported as indicating that the dominion had undertaken to forgo the collection of some $2,272,000 of the principal. That is not correct. The $2,272,000 has been collected from the province already by way of deductions from payments to the province-

under the tax agreements, leaving $14,196,788 still due, the settlement of which has been arranged in the manner 1 have indicated.
The matter, I think, has been settled on a basis satisfactory to both the dominion and the province, and my hope is that future relations between the dominion and the province in regard to this matter will be harmonious and cooperative, and that there will be no further dispute or misunderstanding arising out of the seed grain loans.

speechtext: The purpose of this amendment is to enlarge the War Charities Act to include war memorials as projects acceptable for registration. PROVISION FOR APPROPRIATION OF §1,365,000,000 FOR WAR PURPOSES, DEMOBILIZATION, PROMOTION OF TRADE AND INDUSTRY, ETC.
The house resumed from Friday, September 28, consideration of the motion of Mr. Ilsley that the house go into committee to consider a resolution to grant to His Majesty certain sums of money for the carrying out of measures deemed necessary or advisable in consequence of the war.

Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to speak on this resolution, although. I did have it in mind that I might ask a few questions when the house had resolved itself into committee of the whole. However, the statement made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) before leaving for other parts of the world, and the statement of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) which followed in respect to this resolution, along with the subsequent debate, has led me to desire to say just a word.
I think we should recognize that this resolution is important. It asks for permission to call upon the Canadian people for the tidy sum of 81,365,000.000. There was a day when a few million dollars used to stagger us, but now we have reached the stage of astronomical figures; we talk in terms of billions, and it does not seem to bother us. The wide variety of subjects which this resolution covers means that this money can be raised and spent for almost anything the government may desire to spend it on. It may involve even diplomatic relations; it may involve matters of international trade and commerce, the setting up of diplomatic staffs in other parts of the world, and so forth.
I recognize that Canada does not live in a world by itself. Throughout the past few years Canada has gradually come to be

recognized as one of the leading nations of the world, at least one of the leading small nations. I am not going to say that some credit is not due to the present Prime Minister in that respect, but I am afraid that when it comes to Canada's position in the world, particularly in the future world, sometimes the subject is talked of with some gloss and rather glibly, and terms are used that have not a great deal of reality. For instance, we hear from many sources, not the least being the lips of the Prime Minister, from time to time that we must cooperate in order to bring about a world community of nations. The words "cooperate", "cooperation" and "good will" are very agreeable terms to use. Perhaps I shall deal with them a little later.
There is another word that is used quite often in a glib fashion, and that is "aggression". When most people talk of aggression they always fancy that it is some other nation that is responsible for the aggression, just as though Germany and Italy and Japan, who just happened to be our enemies in war, are the only aggressors in the world. We must be realistic in the use of these terms.
Another word used quite often is "nationalism". Every man believes in his own country, but when he attempts to put his own country in order, or declares publicly that he believes his first duty is to his own country, he is immediately branded as an isolationist or an ultra-nationalist. Then the old propaganda machine gets going and the mighty and powerful propagandists lash out with their lying tongues against him. Social Creditors have been roasted for their stand, but what they really stand for is readiness to cooperate with the world, but at the same time giving to Canada what rightfully belongs to her.
The Prime Minister was in Edmonton not so many months ago. It happened to be during a political campaign, and I know that what is said during a political campaign always must be taken with a grain of salt. But it was the Prime Minister of Canada who was speaking. As he was in Edmonton, the capital city of Alberta, he could not leave alone the Social Crediters who have occupied seats in this house for almost the last ten years. His speech was recorded by the Canadian Press. By the way, before he attacked Alberta he took a nice little tap at a gentleman by the name of John Bracken. He said:
I have not been devoting my time as organizer of a political party.
Of course we know what he meant. What had he been doing?
I wiped out politics when this war began.
That is quite a statement.

War and Demobilization
A rich one.
A complete lie!

Yes; nothing was further from the truth than that statement is.
Let me deal for a moment with this charge that we are ultra-nationalists, that the Social Credit party seem "determined to uphold what they describe as national sovereignty in its most extreme form."
Let me ask, Mr. Speaker, what sovereignty is? Sovereignty simply means the freedom of the individual. It means the freedom of the individual to act as an individual soul in his own right and in his own sphere, free from any big bosses at the top. Sovereignty means that a municipality should be able to act freely within its own sphere and that a province should be able to act according to its own will within its own sphere. Sovereignty means that Canada as a nation should be absolutely free to act as its will chooses within its own sphere. That is what we as Social Crediters have been saying. That is what we believe national sovereignty to mean, and I ask, would any man stand up in this house and say that there is anything wrong with that? You may call me an isolationist, a nationalist, if you like; but personally I am proud to be a Canadian. Personally I think that the duty of members of parliament is to tell the people of this country that our first duty is towards them as Canadians-and if that is being a nationalist, then call us nationalists and we shall be proud of it.
The Prime Minister said that we consistently ignored the vital necessity of external trade to the prosperity and welfare of Canada, and particularly of Alberta. The truth is, Mr. Speaker, that over the years we have disagreed with the Prime Minister's particular policy of seeking world markets as the only solution of
our internal problems. That is where we have differed with the Prime Minister. I do not like to bring in the hungry thirties, because the term and the references have been worn almost threadbare. But where was the Prime Minister and his government in those days when Canada was richly favoured with a vast abundance of good things, when we had almost everything our hearts could desire, when goods were piled upon our shelves and in our warehouses and in our stores, and yet the people were virtually beggars? What was the aim of the Prime Minister's foreign policy then? He looked around for foreign, markets. He said to the world, in effect: Come along, you nations, we have many good things to sell to you here; will you buy?
We might have crept up behind the Prime Minister and pulled his coat-tails and said to him: Mr. Prime Minister, look around. If he had looked around he would have seen thousands of people in Canada on relief and in a state of malnutrition or starvation. What we were trying to do was to pull the Prime Minister's coat-tails a little harder so that he would see these people and so that we could say to him: What are you going to do about these people? Our policy was that you do not have to be entirely dependent upon foreign markets to be able to distribute the goods we have in Canada to our own needy people. The difference between the two parties was this: The Prime Minister wanted to sell Canada to the rest of the world, while the Social Crediters wanted to give Canada to the Canadian people. If that is what the Prime Minister means by saying that we are distin-terested in foreign trade, then I will accept the charge; I do not mind it a bit. But I say to hon. members that what we were trying to tell the Prime Minister was this: We can offer our surpluses to the world, certainly we can, and yet at the same time by proper management of our monetary system we can also give to the Canadian people one of the highest standards of living in the world.
The world trade policy of the Prime Minister was simply this, to use a homely illustration. It does not matter how many eggs we have to fry; we must first feed the whole world with eggs before we can be permitted to fry our own. That was just about the Prime Minister's position with respect to foreign trade.
Of course, on that occasion the Prime Minister also had to tell the people of Alberta why we were not included on the San Francisco delegation. I do not say that he stated it as baldly as that. ,This is what he said, and I am quoting from the same dispatch:
War and Demobilization

Mr. King said it was true Social Credit members voted for participation in the San Francisco conference, but their position was hedged about with qualifications. He quoted John Blackmore, Social Credit house leader, as saying the only voices raised against the proposals for the San Francisco conference had been those of Social Credit members.
What does the Prime Minister expect from members of parliament? Does he expect us to sit here in our chairs, which apparently we are not to be allowed to take home with us, and to acquiesce in all that he says?
Be little yes-men.

Yes; does he expect that? If he does, here is one group that he is going to be sadly disappointed in. Did not the Prime Minister say that he wanted the views of the various parties in the house? Well, we gave him our views, and here is something for other groups to think about. I want you to notice the way his statement reads:
He quoted John Blackmore, Social Credit house leader, as saying the only voices raised against the proposals for the San Francisco conference had been of Social Credit members.
Therefore, says he in effect, I will take on my delegation only those who will not oppose me; the only ones that I want with me are those who will say "yes." That evidently is the truth of the situation, based upon the Prime Minister's own statement. I think other groups in the house should resent that statement. If they do not, they lay themselves open to the charge of being yes-men to the Prime Minister of Canada, who perhaps in the end became yes-man to the world's big power shots.

He surely was, before he went away.

He was not on the question of Argentina. But I was going to say that I regard that as a very minor point in-

deed, because there were other nations which were seeking admission to the San Francisco conference. Let me ask this: Did the same man who objected to one nation raise his voice when the recognized government of Poland were not admitted to the conference?
No, he did not.
Why?
There is a principle involved there. However, I did not intend to get into that discussion.
Neither did they.

The Prime Minister goes
on:
The people of this province who have taken so large a part in the achievement of victory do no-t, I am sure, want the fruits of victory thrown away in political isolationism and economic nationalism.
We want to nail that charge to the wall as a consummate lie. We never did want to throw victory away by any stand we ever took, and that the people recognize this is shown by the fact that we are the only party in the house every one of whose house members was returned in the last election.
Here is another term which is glibly used. You know, if a person rises anywhere in Canada, particularly in a public place, and especially on the floor of this house, and criticizes anything that Russia does, at once he calls down upon his head the anathemas of the red propagandists who saturate nearly all our worth-while institutions, and he is labelled a fascist. Yes, that is the term which is hung on him. Well, I am not so particularly concerned about what I am called. What I am interested in is what I am, and what I am and what I am called are two different things.
In the first place-and I am saying this because I am leading up to another point-I am a Christian. Not because I was bom in England or am a citizen of Canada. I am a Christian because I have explicit and simple faith in the redeeming grace of Almighty God. That is first. Second, I am a Canadian. Being a Christian I must speak the truth in soberness; and being a Canadian I must be loyal to Canada, my country and to the people of Canada.
What I have said brings me to my next point, which relates to this matter of "world cooperation". World cooperation, yes; would anyone rise in this house and say he did not believe in world cooperation? Of course he would not. Would anyone rise and say he was not prepared to work towards world cooperation? Of course he would not. But we

War and Demobilization
must be realistic when we use these terms- "world cooperation", "good will", "world community", "the fuller life", and so forth and so on. For cooperation is not a one way street; it must work two ways. The fact of the matter is that there are two great philosophies struggling for expression and bidding for world recognition. We can talk about a world community and world cooperation, but wherever the world's diplomats meet, be it at San Francisco, Bretton Woods, Dumbarton Oaks, Teheran, Yalta, Potsdam or anywhere else, the one big question is, must God have His way in the world, or must those forces of anti-God have their way in the world? We are not selling peanuts when we go to these great conferences where the world's mighty men meet. Behind the scenes of human activity the greatest battle of the ages is going on. It is a battle for the destiny of worlds of men and nations; it is a battle between the forces of righteousness and the forces of evil. Now when it comes to a matter of cooperation, good cannot cooperate with evil. You had better put that down as a fundamental principle; it cannot be done. That which is Christian cannot cooperate with that which is anti-Christian. Do we want a Christian democracy, or do we want a world with God ruled out? That is the question that should be answered.
The other day the Prime Minister made a statement in the house-and while I am a severe critic of the Prime Minister in his political actions-I do have some respect for him just the same; I am not going to say I have not. I believe he is sincere and desires to do that which is right. Mark you, I will say this too: what I have already said about these forces the Prime Minister knows. My own personal view is that he is cognizant of these things and that he is not insincere in his recognition of them. I do not know, but I do not believe that he told us all that was in his mind when he made his statement in the house the other day.

That would make some
reading.

Well, I do not think that I need any levity at this particular moment. I mean what I say. I believe the Prime Minister is conscientious in respect to those forces, shall I say, of the unknown world, if I can put it that way, and I believe he wants to do the right thing. His intentions may be good. This is what he said in his statement the other day as reported at page 492 of Hansard:
The task is not one of restoring the world as we knew it before the war.
I am inclined to think that he is going off into ethereal platitudes here, because we could ask him in what way the world has changed and I do not think that he could give us an answer. He says:
The task is not one of restoring the world as we knew it before the war. That world has gone. The collective task is to get the new world moving along paths that will lead to peace, happiness and the general welfare.
Then farther on he says:
I feel that I should see for myself something of the changed world in which Canada must make her way and take her part.
It is a very pleasant thing to talk about a changed world, but personally I cannot see that the fundamental and underlying principles that govern this world have changed at all. The only things that have changed so far as I can see, are the geographical and political boundaries. Apart from that, the world philosophies are still intact. The method by which we carry on our foreign trade is still intact. You may make a little adjustment here or a little adjustment there, but there is a great attempt to solidify the world trading facilities under one great and powerful international body, which is attempting to put us back on the gold standard, whereby no nation will be free to trade as it shall choose to trade unless it goes through those channels. And in that regard Canada is in danger of selling out her sovereignty.
How can we have what I should like to call a world Christian democracy? Can a Christian democracy cooperate in any way with totalitarianism? Personally I do not think it can. Jesus denounced the scribes and pharisees as hypocrites, but they were no more hypocrites than our ultra-internationalists who assume a sort of self-righteous attitude, and with their platitudinous phrases about world cooperation attempt to play into the hands of a programme to set up one huge world dictatorship. Can we cooperate with totalitarianism? Can we, as a democracy, cooperate with dictatorship? Dictatorship and totalitarianism mean the loss of freedom. Totalitarianism means force. It means compulsion; it means war; it means murder; it means plunder; it means political and economic gansterism. Therefore I ask the question, can any Christian democracy-if we put down as a fundamental thesis that we are one-cooperate with that?
I hold in my hand a clipping which contains the statement of a great man. This man, speaking before a certain body, said:
With many of you. I hoped that Russia would work out its own problems and that their government would eventually become a peace-loving
War and Demobilization

popular government with a free ballot which would not interfere with the integrity of its neighbours.
That hope is to-day either shattered or put away in storage against a better day.
The Soviet Union, as a matter of practical fact, is a dictatorship as absolute as any other dictatorship in the world.
Who said that? None other than President Roosevelt, speaking before the American youth conference in Washington in 1940.
What is the record of this totalitarian state?
1.	This state provoked, directed and supported civil war and aggression in Spain. They may have claimed the right to do so, I do not know; nevertheless that is what they did.
2.	This state concluded a treaty of nonaggression with Germany in August 1939, an act which enabled Hitler to launch his offensive. Perhaps they will say they had a legal right to do so. I am not arguing the point.
3.	From September, 1939, until June, 1941, this totalitarian state supplied Germany with various essential materials such as food and oil products.
4.	On September 17, 1939, this state committed an act of aggression against Poland, thus violating a treaty of non-aggression concluded with that country.
6.	Having occupied part of Poland, this state deported Polish citizens into various remote parts of Russia and confined them to concentration and labour camps under most inhuman conditions, comparable to those prevailing in German concentration camps.
6.	Following the partition of Poland this state committed acts of aggression against Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia, deprived them of their independence, and subjected the populations to a rule of terror. Soviet Russia waged a war of aggression against Finland, violating the existing treaties.
7.	In all countries of eastern and southeastern Europe Soviet authorities are behaving in a way which does not differ from that of nazi Germany.
I have placed those seven points on record and I ask: Can we as a democracy cooperate with that? Just the other day I picked up the daily paper on my way down to the house and read an Associated Press despatch from Warsaw. I will not read it all, but here is part of it:
War-ravaged Poland is experiencing one of the greatest migrations in her long turbulent history, and two bridges across the Vistula here are the teeming gateways to the east and the west. . . .
fMr. Hansel!.]
From early morning until midnight there is a steady stream of men, women and children carrying all their worldly possessions strapped to their backs, in bags, in suitcases and in sacks.
All faces show lines of strain and work. Scarcely one, whether he is going east or west, has the slightest idea of where he will finally settle. They only know this has to be done, and they tramp on.
I ask: can we cooperate with that? I hear also glibly stated the term "liberation"-

speechtext: Order. I must inform the hon. gentleman that his time has expired.

Well, Mr. Speaker, I
suppose I shall have to stop. Even if I were given permission to go on it would take me another two hours at least to say all I should like to say, so I shall abide by your ruling. I expect I shall be able to say what I have to say at another time, but I want the house to know that I am not through with this subject.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I am sure they would respond, and one which would help them realize that this challenge is just as great as was the challenge of war.
I was pleased to-day to hear the Minister of Finance, in his capacity of Acting Prime Minister, table an order in council setting up a Canadian information service. In saying this I do not necessarily approve the extent to which we now have government by order in council, but I do approve the step taken. I know-at least I suspect-that my hon. friends to the right who belong to the Progressive Conservative party will say that this new organization is just a continuation of the wartime information board, and the chances are that they will oppose it.
The hon. member is not a mind reader.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Well, I shall leave it to them; but it is not long ago that the hon. member for Lake Centre was asking that the wartime information board be discontinued. I take it that board has now ended its days and has been replaced by the Canadian information service. It would seem that the name is modelled after a similar set-up in Great Britain, where the name "British information service" is used. I hope the government will not listen too carefully to the pleas made by hon. members to my right against these public information institutions. In a democracy we cannot have too much information, and the activities of the wartime information board were all to the good.
In my view such institutions as the national film board and the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation should not be limited by suspicion on the part of some on the opposition side of the house that they are used for purposes of political propaganda. Rather they should be given a freer hand to increase the dissemination of information of all kinds, not only in other countries but throughout Canada as well.
One task I should like to see the government give the new Canadian information service, the film board and the CBC, would be one in which those organizations would have a free hand to place before the Canadian people the importance of the task of rehabilitating war-torn Europe. In other words, let us get on with the job of supporting wholeheartedly the work of UNRRA, which got off to such a good start, but which, it seems to me, has been allowed to bog down under officialdom and red tape.
Not long ago Professor Earl G. Harrison, who is dean of the university of Pennsylvania law school, and a former immigration commissioner of the United States, was appointed by President Truman to act on a special

committee to investigate conditions under which people are living in Europe, with special reference to the plight of the Jewish people. In his report, which was published, in the New York Times of Sunday, September 30, two days ago, Professor Harrison had a number of comments to make about UNRRA. The report is a lengthy one, and I shall not load Hansard with quotations from it. Professor Harrison makes it clear that UNRRA is trying to do a good job, but that it is handicapped by lack of competent and efficient personnel in the areas in which its work is being carried on. He points out further that it is hampered by a lack of the kind of cooperation which should exist between UNRRA and the military authorities. The whole picture is one of a noble idea failing for lack of the support it should have. All of this underlies the point I am trying to make, namely, that we have not yet had the imagination to see in UNRRA just as great a challenge as we had in the war itself. In fact, the challenge is really far greater.
I am not criticizing the government for anything it has done in connection with UNRRA, and most certainly I am not criticizing the Minister of Finance when he asks for $25 million. That sum is far too small, and my criticism is that we in Canada have not done enough for this organization. It has been treated as a sort of step-child in the hope that somehow it will grow up and be able to do the job assigned to it. The other day the Minister of Finance made this statement about the $25 million he is asking for UNRRA under the terms of the resolution now before the house. I quote from page 564 of Hansard for September 28:
This is intended to enable us to furnish, before the end of our fiscal year, a portion of a second contribution to UNRRA, which the Canadian government has agreed to make, provided that the United States and other contributing nations will also make a second contribution.
I suppose that that is the way a minister of the crown would put it, and that is the way governments have to act. I do feel, however, that Canada should be not holding back in this fashion and saying; We wall do so and so, provided that somebody else does his part.
The fate of civilization depends upon whether or not our generation has the imagination and the capacity to rehabilitate a world which we have had to tear apart by war. I plead with those in authority, with the government and with parliament, to face the seriousness of the question. I urge that we do our best not only here but in our constituencies and throughout the country to

War and Demobilization
arouse interest in UNRRA and other related activities. We have here some of the most glorious opportunities for service ever presented to any generation.
I take second place to no one in my concern for the people of Canada. Hon. members will recognize the persistence with which I have pleaded the lot of old age pensioners, and all citizens of this country whose problems need to be fought on the floor of this house. Hon. members will recall the fights I make for housing, and for the improvement of many adverse conditions found here in Canada. But alongside of that I emphasize the fact that it is useless for us to try to build up our own standard of living and our own situation here in this dominion if we are to let the world go to rack and ruin, as will happen if something is not done about living conditions in the countries that have been tom by war.
As I indicated when I rose, in speaking of the plight of the peoples in Europe I took as my motif the fact that none of us is free so long as there is bondage or slavery anywhere. I want to say a word especially about the plight of the Jewish people in Europe. I have referred already to the Harrison report which was made to President Truman, the full text of which appeared in last Sunday's New York Times. Professor Harrison summed up the plight of the Jewish people in Europe at the present time when he said to President Truman:
As matters now stand, we appear to be treating the Jews as the nazis treated them, except that we do not exterminate them. They are in concentration camps in large numbers under our military guard instead of S.S. troops. One is led to wonder whether the German people, seeing this, are not supposing that we are following or at least condoning nazi policy.
That is a terrible statement. Professor Harrison gives the details of what he meant. He relates stories of the barbed wire behind which many Jews are still languishing. He describes the horrible plight of these people, hungry, displaced, not knowing where their friends and relatives are, many of them without medical care or adequate clothing. Some of these people, to their chagrin, are forced to wear German S.S. uniforms, with the result that they are subject to all kinds of abuse. Hon. members will have noticed from the press that President Truman was greatly exercised over this report and that he has given orders to General Eisenhower to take immediate steps to see that something is done about the whole situation.
It does seem to some of us that it is a sad state of affairs that this race of people, who have been the pawns of so many cross-currents and conflicts down through the history of
mankind, should once again, just at a time when we thought we had finished with the horrors of war and were about to begin to build a new world, find themselves facing such hopeless and pitiful circumstances. I feel that I am only being human in rising in this parliament of Canada to express the hope that something will be done without delay to provide relief for these people from the sufferings they are undergoing.
Professor Harrison makes a number of recommendations in his report. The one he makes most strongly in that President Truman use his good offices to secure the abrogation of the MacDonald white paper of 1939 which prohibited, with a slight exception for five years, Jewish immigration to Palestine. Those who have been following the press on this point will know what has happened in the past few days. They will know that President Truman and Prime Minister Attlee have been in correspondence on this whole matter. We all recognize what a thorny question it is because of the position the Arabs are taking with respect to any change in Palestine policy. Incidentally I hold in my hand copies of an exchange of telegrams between the Mufti of Jerusalem and Hitler regarding the war in north Africa, made at a time when the armies of Rommel were rolling westward. I should like to quote the last sentence in one of the Mufti's telegrams to Hitler. It reads:
The Arab people will further continue to fight on your side against the common enemy up to ultimate victory.
I suggest that these are not people to whom we should be applying any policy of appeasement; yet I am not one to belittle the tremendous problem facing those who are concerned about the situation in the Balkans, the Mediterranean and the near east. The whole question is one that should lie heavily on the conscience of the world. Hon. members will recognize my wholehearted support of the government now in power in Great Britain, and in saying that I speak for the whole of this group. But we insist that the British government must carry out its pledge to re-open Palestine to Jewish immigration. The leader of this group, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), to-day issued a press release in which he said in part:
The C.C.F. has officially stated its opposition to the unfair and discriminatory white paper. The permission for fifteen hundred Jews to enter Palestine monthly is pathetically inadequate for their needs. They must be allowed to enter their national homeland in larger numbers. Only in Palestine have they been permitted to build a progressive and cooperative society. Their record there, in terms of both social and economic justice, speaks for itself.

The C.C.F. has sent cables to the Right Honourable Clement Attlee, Prime Minister of Great Britain, and to Morgan Phillips, secretary of the British Labour party, urging that the British government give every consideration to a revised white paper which will provide European Jewry with the freedom to migrate to, and live in the mandated territory of Palestine.
The leader of this group sent that out on our behalf, and I take this occasion to say that we believe the hands of the British government need to be strengthened in this matter. We feel they are right in saying that any action which might result in trouble- I believe such threats are only a bluff, but the possibility has to be faced-should be taken as a joint responsibility by the British people and the people of the United States, perhaps indeed by the peoples of all the united nations. It is because I feel that the British government should have its hands strengthened in its effort to do the right thing in connection with this matter that I raise my voice in this parliament. I dare to assume that most hon. members will agree with me that the doors of Palestine should be opened, and that these people, who, God knows, have suffered down through the years far more than any human beings should have had to suffer, should get some relief from the terrible conditions which they have had to face in Europe during these last few years, and which, sad to say, appear to exist in Europe even at the present time.
I hope that the government of this country will interest itself in this whole matter and, along with the United States, declare to the British government its readiness to stand with them in connection with any policy that that government feels it should take for improving the position of these people.

Would the
hon. member go so far as to say that Canada should provide soldiers to fight the Arabs to protect these people, if it should come to that?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: That is the kind of question which it is difficult to answer because it is hypothetical, for I firmly believe that the position taken by the Arabs is one of bluff.
Is the hon. member aware that only within the last week the British government has had to send a parachute division to Palestine?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I am quite aware of that. I am also aware of the complications that have arisen because of the position taken by certain sections in India with respect to this whole question. I could indulge in a cross-fire argument, Mr. Speaker, but that is something I am anxious to avoid at this time.

I was not
being critical at all.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I fully recognize that.
My reason for trying to avoid argument is that I am trying to put this matter on such a plane that it will command unanimous support. The hon. gentlemen who have questioned me know what their own answers would be, but even so I detected in their words a note of sympathy with the position I am taking, and I pass that sympathy along to the government of the day.
I want to speak for a moment or two about another matter which, although on first thought, it may seem to be unrelated to what I have been discussing, is closely connected with this whole question of our playing some part in relieving the suffering that the war has left in its wake around the world. We cannot play our part simply by a national clothing collection such as we are having this month, no matter how much effort we put into that campaign. If we are to play our part in helping to rehabilitate war-tom Europe we should seek to maintain the level of production in this country at its war-time height, and so I urge again upon the government that it reconsider its whole policy of reconversion and its plans with regard to post-war employment. As I study the government's plans and try to see their point of view, it seems to me that they are thinking too much in terms of the needs of this country solely on the basis of the income that our people have or may have during the next few years. We should be planning our production not only to meet the needs of the people of this country, but also to be able to render some real contribution to the rehabilitation of war-torn countries.
In that connection I think, for example, of a plant like MacDonald Brothers aircraft factory in Winnipeg, which instead of being more or less idle to-day might be used for the making of prefabricated houses for shipment to these countries. It is a tremendous undertaking, Mr. Speaker, if one lets his imagination play upon it, for us to make the kind of contribution that I envisage. But I come back to this. What we undertook in the war was a tremendous task. If the Minister of Finance or the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply had been told in 1939 that under their direction, if you want to put it that way, we would be producing in this country the volume of goods and services and munitions and supplies that we did produce in 1943 and 1944, I doubt that they would have believed it possible for us to do it. But it was undertaken because of the necessity of the task that lay before us. There is now the task of rebuilding

War and Demobilization
the world which we have torn asunder, and we now should be producing with the same determination that we displayed during the war. My contention is that the whole question of what shall be done with war plants, and our plans for reconversion, production and employment, should be worked out not just in terms of our own internal economy, but in terms also of what we can do to meet the needs of the world as they face us at the present time.
I might call to the attention of 'the government-I shall not take time to go into detail -the representations that have been made by both the major labour congresses in this country on reconversion and employment. I would urge upon the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply-I hope they will not think I am actuated by political considerations, because I am very serious-that Canada play its maximum part in producing sufficient goods and services to help rebuild the world and give us a chance to achieve the peace which we hope will be permanent after all the sacrifices we have gone through during these past six years.

May I ask by what means the hon. member proposes that the government should raise the money with which to buy the products of all these Canadian factories so as to render them available to the peoples of the world, perhaps through some such scheme as UNRRA?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
The government did not have much difficulty in raising the money, as the hon. member himself has often pointed out to the Minister of Finance, to purchase the supplies required for war. In fact, year after year when the Minister of Finance brought down his budget he simply borrowed the money that was required to balance the budget, partly from the chartered banks and partly from the Bank of Canada. The Minister of Finance himself said many a time- I note that he is in his seat and can correct me if I am wrong-that the huge expenditures of money we were making were not to be regarded as sums taken from a board which had to be put back, but were an index of our greatly increased production. When hon. members to my right and to my left have taunted the Minister of Finance about the size of the national debt, his reply has always been that if we would keep up our level of production we could handle any national debt that might develop under his financial leadership. I have my own. ideas which I could go into if there were time, but I simply say that I think that the experience of the war years, even under a Liberal capitalist administration, has shown that it can be done if only we have the will.
This is coming dangerously close to a political discussion, but I think hon. members will recognize from the tone of my remarks that I rose to-day not for such a purpose, but to speak on what seems to me is the task before us at this time, namely, that we should be gearing our economic activities, our production and our reconversion programme, not only to improving the standing of living in Canada, but also to playing our maximum part in the rebuilding of a war-tom world.
Would I be safe in assuming from the hon. member's reply that he would favour adding to the national debt of Canada at the colossal rate to which we have become accustomed during the war?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
The hon. member is not safe in assuming that at all. My quarrel with the Minister of Finance is that while I believe his declaration to be true that our huge war expenditures have been only an index of our increased production, he has permitted that index-simply a matter of figures-to be turned into additions to the national debt on which interest has to be paid for all time. That means taking a portion out of the national income each year from now on and giving it to a privileged few, which as I see it is completely unrealistic, and fails to recognize the basic factors in the production of goods and services, which are human labour and raw material.
I have had quite a bit to say about our producing and sending overseas supplies of one kind and another. There is one kind of material, however, which I hope Canada will stop sending to certain countries I could name. I confess, despite the explanations about it in the press which I have seen from the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon), to considerable concern over the shipment of aluminum to Spain this year. I am not going to make an issue out of it at this point, or debate it at length, but I want to put on record the fact of such shipment as it was contained in sessional paper 145 tabled yesterday by the Minister of Trade and Commerce in response to questions which I had placed on the order paper. In this return the minister indicates that from January 1 to August 31, 1945, Canada shipped aluminum in bars, blocks, ingots, sheets, et cetera, to Spain, in the amount of 4,408,500 pounds. That is the fifth largest quantity sent to the various countries to which we exported aluminum this year. I may make it a little plainer: we have exported aluminum to twenty countries thus far in 1945. The largest quantities have gone to the United Kingdom, the United States, Russia and

Vf ar and Demobilization

Switzerland, and the next largest is to Spain. Bearing in mind the political situation in Spain, and the experiences we have had with that country over the last number of years; bearing in mind too-I will try to say this with all the reserve of which I am capable, but I feel very deeply about it-the years past when we shipped scrap iron and other war materials to aggressor nations, I cannot but be deeply concerned that already we should be shipping this material, which is so useful in war, to a fascist nation. I hope that some member of the government will explain this, or, better still, indicate to us that it will be stopped. Let us this time refrain from sending war materials to any country which might use them for further aggression.
With that reservation, Mr. Speaker, I urge with all the power that I can that the government, parliament and the country put its shoulder to the wheel and get on with the tremendous task and the great opportunities which are presented to us in the aims and activities of UNRRA.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to take part in this debate because I want to discuss one point which has already been raised; but before I come to that particular point, in view of the fact that a week-end has intervened since this debate started, and yesterday was private members' day, I crave the indulgence of hon. members while I run over some of the matters which have been raised, in order to make clear the subject with which I wish to deal.
In introducing this resolution the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley) pointed out that we were being asked to approve the raising of a great deal of money, and at the present time the main purpose, as I understood it, was that the defence estimates might be got through.
The hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) followed. Speaking, I might say, on behalf of the official opposition, he outlined the four principles which we feel should govern Canada in her attitude toward defence matters. The four principles, I should like to recall to hon. members, were: first, that Canada should maintain sufficient forces to guarantee the defence of Canada and also to enable us to fulfil whatever might be our commitments to the united nations organization; second, that the efficiency of those forces must be our prime consideration; third, that the forces must be allied with scientific developments; fourth, that there should be the maximum coordination of developments and practice with Great Britain and the United States in
rMr. Knowles.]
respect of our armed forces. Finally he suggested that there should be a parliamentary committee on defence along the lines of the military and naval affairs committees of the United States congress, in order that hon. members might be better informed as to the requirements for defence and keep the people of Canada better informed on these subjects.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), I am glad to say, supported in principle all the suggestions which had been outlined by the hon. member for Vancouver South. We had further talks from the leader of the Social Credit group in this house (Mr. Low) and from the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker), both of whom spoke in very fine terms of the prospects of peace under the united nations charter. The hon. member for Lake Centre directed the attention of the house to the question whether the moneys which we are to be asked to vote will be expended exclusively under orders in council under the terms of the emergency War Measures Act. He asked the specific question, is the war at an end? Do the provisions of the emergency War Measures Act govern all our actions? That is the point with which I wish to deal this afternoon.
I was going to base my stand on the statement that it is time, in my view, that we restore to parliament all its liberties and its privileges and recover in full the democratic system of government. I must confess that I had some doubts put into my mind in listening to the speech of the hon. member for Ros-thern (Mr. Tucker) when we were supposed to be discussing the question of the relief of settlers under the Soldiers Settlement Act, and he discussed Liberal candidates and how it was that he and the other Liberal members for Saskatchewan had been elected; how it was that the hon. member for Lake Centre was elected, and then the question of the size of families and the amounts of payments under the Family Allowances Act; and we even discussed-

I defer to your ruling. I was not trying to reopen the discussion; I was merely referring to it in connection wdth my own point. However, I will pass on to other matters.
Dealing directly with the question of whether or not we should allow ourselves to be governed under the provisions of the War Measures Act, I wish to refer again to the wording of that act. We find these words in section 6 of the act. I should like to explain

that after certain powers have been conferred, or perhaps after certain powers exercisable by the governor in council have been outlined in sections 3, 4 and 5 of the act, section 6 goes on to say:
The provisions of the three sections last preceding shall only be in force during war, invasion, or insurrection, real or apprehended.
I wish to make it clear that it is only during war, invasion or insurrection that the powers exercisable under the emergency War Measures Act can be fairly invoked. How do we decide whether a state of war, invasion or insurrection exists? I shall refer hon. members to the provisions of section 2 of the act which reads as follows:
The issue of a proclamation by His Majesty, or under the authority of the governor in council shall be conclusive evidence that war, invasion, or insurrection, real or apprehended, exists . . .
The section goes on to say that:
. . . until by the issue of a further proclamation it is. declared that the war, invasion, or insurrection no longer exists.
Therefore we are in this position, that the decision as to whether or not a state of war, invasion or insurrection exists is squarely up to the governor in council, a matter to be decided by the cabinet. I would direct the attention of the responsible ministers and of all hon. members to the fact that it is not a question of whether or not a state of emergency exists; there is no mention of emergency in the act in that connection. It is a question of whether or not a state of war, invasion or insurrection exists.
I should like to remind hon. members again that there is a great deal of significance attached to this question; because if it is decided that a state of war, invasion or insurrection exists, then certain things can be done by order in council, for instance, all the things which are to be done under the provisions of the bill, the resolution for which is now before the house. I should like to read the provisions of that resolution which are to be found at page 546 of Hansard-.
Hon. J. L. Ilsley (Minister of Finance) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure *to provide, inter alia . . .
I shall read only part of the resolution, but I should like to make it clear that the parts I am leaving out do not alter the sense.
1. That sums ... be granted to His Majesty towards defraying any expenses . . . that may be incurred . . . under the authority of the governor in council . . . for
(a) the security, defence, peace, order and welfare of Canada.

Those are very wide terms. Under the terms of the resolution there is very little that cannot be done by order in council. Consider the wording "the security, defence, peace, order and welfare of Canada". These words give to the cabinet even wider powers than are given to the dominion parliament under section 91 of the British North America Act. I should like to read the relevant words of section 91, which read as follows:
It shall be lawful for the queen, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and House of Commons . . .
To enact these things:
... to make laws for the peace, order, and good government of Canada.
We now have it "for the security, defence, peace, order and welfare of Canada." These powers are as wide as, in fact they are wider than, the powers originally given to parliament under the British North America Act. Further, the resolution contains these powers:
.	.	. for the carrying out of any measure
deemed necessary or advisable by the governor in council in consequence of the war.
If we allow that sort of thing to continue we are completely, and possibly for all time, surrendering the rights of parliament; we are giving to the governor in council powers for making and carrying out any measure deemed necessary or advisable in consequence of the war. That covers everything.
I again read from the terms of the resolution :
For the expeditious demobilization of the Canadian armed forces.
That is to be carried out by order in council. Do we wish, Mr. Speaker-and I ask hon. members to consider this carefully- to entrust the cabinet with all the power to make every regulation with regard to demobilization? I submit that if we do so we are denying the democratic principle of responsible government. Under that system we are the ones who are supposed to decide on the validity or advisability of any measure introduced by the government of Canada, or any detail of the government of this country. Although under certain circumstances we may be justified in surrendering our responsibilities or handing over our responsibilities for a limited time, we are only justified in handing them over to those who by their attitude and actions show that they themselves are responsible persons and will safeguard the rights and privileges that we ourselves have put into their safekeeping. I suggest to the careful consideration of hon. members that we should not hand over the powers to make final and complete regulations for the de-
War and Demobilization

mobilization of our armed forces when the minister himself seems reluctant to assume the responsibility of making those regulations, when he seeks as he sought in this house on September 24 to hand over the .responsibility to a general of the armed forces. I submit that is putting us in a position where, if we criticize the decisions taken, we are criticizing an officer overseas, not a responsible officer of the department, but an officer in charge of the armed forces. That is a denial of the principle of responsible government, and for my part I am not willing to hand over those responsibilities which I should exercise, if they are to be exercised in that manner.
In considering further the matter of demobilization of our armed forces I would ask this question:	For whom did those forces
fight, for the cabinet ministers, or for Canada? I think the answer is obvious, that they fought for Canada. Then, I suggest that it is up to us, the elected representatives of Canada and of those armed forces, to see to it that the regulations for their demobilization are approved by us before they are put into effect. If we adopt the other attitude I suggest we are going to allow all matters of defence policy to be determined by order in council.
Here I wish to refer to an incident which took place the other day. I should like to read an article which appeared in the Ottawa Journal of September 29, 1945. The dispatch is dated Vancouver, September 28, and reads:
Canada's peace-time navy, "much larger" than before the war, will be divided evenly between the Atlantic and Pacific coasts, it was announced here to-day by Rear Admiral V. C. Brodeur, R.C.N., commanding officer, Pacific coast.
Admiral Brodeur said at a press conference the post-war navy will include cruisers, aircraft carriers, destroyers and frigates but no corvettes. Ships, men and training facilities would be divided fifty-fifty basis between the two coasts.
I will not read the whole dispatch, but this officer went on to describe in detail the constitution of the navy. This is the most -complete statement of policy to have been made available to this house as yet on the subject of naval affairs; and this statement of policy came not from the responsible minister of the department or a responsible official, but from a naval officer in Vancouver, some three thousand miles away from this building, although the naval estimates were scheduled to come up first and the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) had asked for an over-all statement of defence policy, which as yet he has not received. We were supposed to discuss and consider those estimates; that was our responsibility, but the only clue we are given is in this statement, made in Vancouver.

I realize that perhaps it does not do for a new member to come here and appear to lecture the house or responsible ministers of the crown, and I pause here to make sure to myself that I am not standing up here lecturing. I had certain ideas as to the responsibility of my job when I should come here, and as to the seriousness of that responsibility. I am surprised and alarmed to find that under the present set-up, so long as we have a continuation of this system of government by order in council, however well intentioned may be the motives behind those orders in council, I am not exercising my responsibility; and I feel that I cannot allow this situation to continue without bringing it to the attention of the other members of this house so that we may have an open and frank discussion on this matter and I may be informed in the net result as to whether or not I may have an overdeveloped sense of responsibility. I do not think I have, and that is why I am bringing this matter into the open.
To continue this discussion, this being the situation: the powers which I have described, and which appear in the terms of this resolution, being available to the government, to be exercised by order in council, with the serious consequences I have indicated in the matter of our own handing-over of responsibility, together with the fact that the existence of this situation depends upon the decision by the cabinet as to whether or not war, invasion or insurrection exists, I think we are entitled to call on the cabinet and on the responsible ministers to consider that question seriously and fairly. When the matter was brought up by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) we saw in the attitude of the ministers of the crown indications that they have not considered it either seriously or fairly. The hon. member for Lake Centre read extracts from an opinion given by the council of the Canadian Bar Association. I should like to refresh the memory of hon. members by reading part of that opinion again:
Your committee is of opinion that the state of war cannot and should not, even by the authority of a statute, be deemed to continue to exist when the war itself is over. Let us make the distinction here between the war emergency itself, which is the fact of a state of war, and an economic emergency which, though a consequence following the war, is not the war emergency itself. If the federal administration feel that there may exist, after the war, in relation to the economic condition of the country, a state of emergency of a most serious character, and national in scope, let them face the issue squarely, and submit to

parliament a new law, so as to affirm the exist; ence, or the apprehension, and determine the exact nature, of that new emergency.
Hon. members will recall the attitude adopted by certain ministers of the crown when the hon. member for Lake Centre read that opinion. They will recall the attitude of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Abbott) and also, I think, the inference correctly drawn therefrom by the hon. member for Lake Centre. I should like to read that exchange, referring to page 577 of Hansard.
Mr. Abbott:	Which member wrote the
opinion ?
A little further down:
Mr. Diefenbaker:	The chairman of the committee was Gustave Monette, K.C., of Montreal.
Mr. Abbott: That is why I asked the question.
Mr. Diefenbaker:	Surely the Minister of
National Defence does not suggest that the following members of the bar . . .
Then he named a list of distinguished members of the bar.
. . . would allow the signing of a report with respect to their understanding of the law to be influenced because a certain man happened to be chairman?
That is the inference drawn from the attitude taken by the Minister of National Defence which, in considering a constitutional question of this importance, I submit was a most irresponsible attitude. Yet this is a member of the cabinet which is asking to have all these powers, exercisable by order in council, vested in it. I should like to read further from the report of the Canadian Bar Association. this time from the report of the committee on legislation affecting civil liberties, as contained in the minutes of the mid-winter council meeting, at page 33:
Your committee reports that no further progress has been made towards obtaining the privilege of viewing legislation in the form of orders in council and board orders prior to adoption, in order that suggestions for the preservation of public rights might be made, niter the experience with order 294 of the rentals administration section of the wartime prices and trade board, where any suggestions along the lines mentioned were invariably ruled out as being interference with policy, it was felt that there was little point in pressing matters as it was obvious that bureaucratic policy and preservation of civil liberties were incompatible. . . .
And further:
Your committee's conclusion must be that there is no hope for relief from this most undemocratic form of dictatorship under the guise of legislation, and that so long as persons having no real responsibility to constitutional forms of government are given the power to regulate the rights of the individual, many of those rights will continue to be subject to the kind of totalitarian rule which the free peoples are fighting to abolish from the world.
That report is signed by R. M. Willes Chitty, in case the Minister of National Defence may be interested. The point I am trying to make here is that responsible persons outside the government, acting in good faith-legal experts-have reviewed this situation and come to certain conclusions. I submit that these conclusions on matters affecting civil liberty should have the most serious consideration of all hon. members of this house, including the members of the cabinet. Therefore I should like to read, for the Minister of National Defence especially, a previous report written while the war emergency existed, and by that I mean while the war was actually going on. This is a report of the same committee on civil liberties, which appears at page 600 of the "Canadian Bar Review" for 1944.
Whatever opinion anyone might have as to any possible abuse by the federal authorities, or their delegated boards, of the wide powers so granted to them, and in spite of the civil encroachments this war legislation has developed against the liberty of the subject, your committee feel that .this association ought not to do anything that might appear to antagonize, or even directly criticize, the principle of full control, during the war, of the citizen, his liberty, property and activities, to the extent that the government deem necessary for the safety of the nation. The government alone have full information of the necessities of the hour, and however well informed we, of this association, may be, we should not assume the risk of embarrassing in the least degree the government of the country in the paramount task of winning the war.
That was an opinion written in 1944, while the war was on, by the same body which submitted in 1945 a report at which the Minister of National Defence scoffs. I do not notice the government crying out against the terms of this report, and therefore I imagine it must be most acceptable to them. I should like to draw to the attention of the minister the fact that this report of 1944 is signed by Gustave Monette, chairman.
Possibly the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) will be pleased to know that, in order to relieve him of any anxiety, I do intend to refer to the statement of the Acting Prime Minister (Mr. Ilsley) in vhich he referred to the setting up of the Canadian information board. At the moment I am not referring to the question whether or not some such information service is desirable; I do not refer to that at all. But I do object most strenuously to the manner of constituting that board, while parliament is in session, when the war emergency has passed. I object to doing this by order in council, and without having referred the matter previously to the house.

After what I have said I would repeat the question asked on Friday last, I believe it was, by the hon. member for Lake Centre. I would ask hon. members to bear in mind what I have said, and the attitude which in my opinion should govern in a situation of this kind. This is what we find at page 576 of Hansard where the hon. member for Lake Centre is questioning the Acting Prime Minister:
Mr. Diefenbaker:	. . . Are we still at war,
within the provisions of the War Measures Act, or are we not? That is the question I am asking.
Mr. Ilsley: The answer is yes.
Mr. Diefenbaker: What is that?
Mr. Ilsley: The answer is yes.
Mr. Diefenbaker: "The answer is yes?"
Mr. Ilsley: Yes.
Mr. Diefenbaker: That is the legal opinion that is given, is it?
Mr. Ilsley: Yes.
Mr. Diefenbaker: That is the legal opinion given by law officers of the crown?
Mr. Ilsley: Yes.
There can be no doubt that in the minds of the members of the cabinet, as represented in the statement of the Acting Prime Minister, we are still at war under the provisions of the War Measures Act, although it must be confessed that we have not yet seen the opinion given by the law officers of the crown.
If this is so, I suggest that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) is not of the same opinion as the other members of his cabinet. His actions, his mental attitude and the precedent he has set are entirely different. In substantiation of that claim I would read to hon. members part of the statement made by the Prime Minister when he told us that he intended to go to the United Kingdom and to other countries in Europe. I submit that the statement of principle outlined by the Prime Minister, which influenced him in arriving at his decision to go over there is an exact statement of those principles which should govern us in asking the government of this country to hand back to us those rights which we voluntarily surrendered in war time.
I would ask hon. members to follow those portions of the Prime Minister's speech, which I shall read, to see if they do not agree with me when I state that the parallel is almost exact. Again I cannot take time to read the whole of the speech made by the Prime Minister on that occasion, but so far as I have been able, in respect of each excerpt I have taken care not to alter the general sense. Turning first to page 492 we find the Prime Minister reported as follows:
The world is still in a very troubled state.
. . . These last months have seen many changes in Europe, brought new persons into responsible office and faced them with new problems.

I submit that exactly the same is true of Canada. Then he continues:
We in Canada are directly concerned with the solutions which they are seeking to these problems.
We in the House of Commons of Canada are very much concerned with the solutions which are found to our Canadian problems. Hon. members will realize that I am quoting from the Prime Minister's speech and then tracing the parallel which I claim appears.
Then, further down on page 492 he says:
In the shaping of the new world order, a good start must be made in the right direction during these next critical months. Decisions that will have to be taken during the coming months may shape and determine the kind of *world we are going to live in.
I submit that exactly the same is true of the situation in Canada. Decisions which are taken in the coming months may determine whether we shall live under a full and free democratic system, or under a system of controls, bureaucracy and semi-totalitarianism.
Then the Prime Minister went on to say that certain questions-
. . . are important, but in the last analysis, many of them are of less consequence, even to the countries whose interests they affect nyjst immediately, than are questions of attitudes and objectives. .	.	. What kind of world do we
really wish to live in? What sort of effort are we ready to make to realize it?
What then, I ask hon. members, is our attitude to responsible government? What is our attitude to democracy? That is the important thing. It is more important even than the fact that something may be done more expeditiously by order in council. That is the frame of mind1 which induced the Prime Minister to take the serious step of leaving this House of Commons, and going to the United Kingdom.
What sort of effort are we making, what sort of effort are we ready to make to realize the kind of world we want to live in? With deference I would ask other hon. members to apply that question to themselves: What sort of effort are we ready to make to get back the power to carry out those rights and duties that are ours, an effort which I submit we can no longer shirk?
Then the Prime Minister goes on to say:
It is important that Canada should not merely be consulted, but that there should be clear recognition of Canada's right to effective participation in the great decisions where questions affecting the genera] ordering of the future peace of the world are under consideration.
It is important that parliament should not be merely consulted, but that there should be a clear recognition of our right to take part in decisions affecting our national life. The
