Prime Minister continues:
During the war, for military reasons, it was necessary to acquiesce in the operation of wartime arrangements under which responsibility for major decisions on the direction of the allied war effort was concentrated in a very few hands.
This is similar to the process of handing over to the cabinet the power of government by order in council. Then he proceeds to say:
The continued use of methods such as were improvised to meet the urgent strain and hazards of war, whereby private settlements are arrived at between the great powers on issues of general interest, might well become a source of difficulty and even of danger.
I submit, finally, that now that the war is over, the continuation of those methods which we voluntarily allowed to be set up for the purpose of winning the war, will certainly become a source of potential danger and difficulty.
I should like to conclude my remarks by saying again that I do not intend to be taken as standing up and lecturing to this house or to the government. But I do feel that, however well intentioned the ministers of the crown may be in continuing to exercise their powers under orders in council, it is the mere fact of the continuation which constitutes the danger, not the motive in the minds of the ministers. I realize, as has been said here so often, that they are under a tremendous burden. They want to get things done expeditiously, quickly and efficiently. For the time being they consider it more efficient to carry on by order in council. We let time go on and the same thing is said again. In the meantime we get into the habit of government by order in council. It seems to be a good method of carrying on government and the ministers become a little more reluctant to part with their powers, but still with the best of motives. That I submit is where the danger lies. I want to make it perfectly clear that I am not questioning the motives of any minister in any of the remarks I have made to-day. I am merely asking the question: Have we not arrived at the stage when we must consider whether a continuation of this procedure offers a greater danger to our final achievement of full democracy than the possible loss of efficiency which may result if we stop government by order in council now?
For myself I am inclined to think the greater danger is in continuing government by order in council. Should the situation which I have in mind ever develop-and it may develop as a result of this practice of government by order in council-then all the sacrifices, all the efforts, all the losses and all the heart-break of the past six years will
have been worthless. Therefore I feel justified in taking the time of this house to ask all hon. members to give serious consideration to this question.
(Translation) Mr. Speaker, I spoke briefly this afternoon on the restoration of the powers of parliament. To my mind parliament is the guardian of all our rights, both individual and civil, and even though we may have agreed, under the stress of war to waive our rights voluntarily, nevertheless, at this time when the emergency period has ended, we must insist upon the restoration of those rights and privileges which are inherent in the democratic system; otherwise, we shall be guilty of having betrayed the democratic cause for which we have fought.
I regret very much that my knowledge of the French language is not yet perfect, but I have begun this week to take lessons. Finally, I ask all my fellow-citizens to believe that I voice their feelings or their thoughts when I say that we should uphold our rights so that the Canadian people may enjoy that democratic freedom which is guaranteed to them under the existing constitution.
Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Minister of Justice) (Translation): May I offer my most sincere congratulations to the hon. member who has just resumed his seat. As regards the statement he made when he informed us that he had begun this week to take French lessons, I must say that this is the second occasion on which I have heard him express himself in French in this house and I am sure that he has not begun the study of that language this week only since he has already acquired a fluency on which I congratulate him most heartily. I wish that he may frequently use the French language when participating in the debates of this house.
(Text) Mr. Speaker, I perhaps should offer a word of explanation for the. fact that it is now twenty minutes to six on Tuesday evening when I rise to answer some questions that were suggested by the <hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) on Friday afternoon as being proper to be asked. I rise at this time because the hon. member finished his speech just about six o'clock on Friday afternoon; yesterday was taken up with matters which were appropriate to be discussed on a private member's day and when I came into the chamber this afternoon I found that Mr. Speaker had arranged for three hon. members to be heard before I could have an opportunity of making any answer. The delay
War and Demobilization

certainly is not because I did not wish to make an answer. The hon. member asked, as reported on page 573 of Hansard-.
When will the proclamation be made that will terminate war in so far as the powers of the War Measures Act are concerned?
Then the hon. member went on to ask if the government suggested that to-day we are in the midst of war. He wanted to know if the minister suggested that it could continue the operation of the War Measures Act for one, two or three years or more hence when the government might by proclamation declare the war to be over. He stated that this was a matter of grave importance to the people of this country, and he wanted to know if powers were being exercised by the government to-day which were beyond the competence of the government to carry into effect.
That certainly is a serious question. It would be a serious situation for the Canadian people if any government undertook to exercise powers for which there was no legal basis. I can quite appreciate the concern that is felt in that regard. However, I think it is proper again to direct attention to the terms of the statute which it was found advisable to enact in 1914 at the time the first great war broke out.
The hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) has expressed his views as to government by order in council, but I am sure that is not just what the hon. member meant. Of course government must be by order in council or by decisions of the ministers composing the council. It is quite a different matter though to have legislation by order in council. I take it that when the hon. member decried government by order in council he meant legislation by order in council. Under the terms of the British North America Act, which states that this country wished to have a constitution modeled upon that of the United Kingdom, it was declared in section 9:
The executive government and authority of and over Canada is hereby declared to continue and be vested in the queen.
That power is exercised by a high officer, styled the Governor General, on advice of the council composed of members responsible to the elected chamber, but the legislative power is to be exercised by His Majesty with the consent of the Senate and the House of Commons. When one complains of government by order in council I take it that what he means is the exercise of legislative powers by the governor in council.
It has been well established that the governor in council has no legislative powers that are not expressly given to him by parliament. He cannot exercise legislative powers without their

being powers delegated to him by some act of parliament. This act of 1914 was passed by a government which was formerly composed of some gentlemen still members of the Progressive Conservative party; they submitted to parliament a bill asking parliament in case of war to edelegate to His Excellency in Council legislative powers that otherwise would have to be exercised by the ordinary procedure of bills introduced into one or other of the houses, read three times in each and adopted in the usual form. That parliament decided that that was a wise thing to do and adopted the statute which is now chapter 206 of the revised statutes of 1927.
There had to be some definite point at which the delegation would commence and at which the delegation would end, and that parliament, not the parliament of which the members of the present government were members but the parliament of 1914, said that the delegation would start when the governor in council proclaimed that a state of war existed; that that proclamation would be conclusive as to the starting point, and that the delegation would continue until the governor in council declared by proclamation that the state of war which brought about the delegation had ceased.
There was a proclamation in September, 1939, that a state of war existed, and that proclamation is still in force. Actual hostilities have ceased, but the state of war still exists at the present time, and that state of war created a situation which had to be dealt with by the exercise of the powers which had been delegated for the purpose under the statute.
Hon. members ask: When are these powers to be handed back? They will not be handed back. They will cease to be exercisable certainly when there is a proclamation saying that the war has ended. They will be diminished; they have been diminishing by the cessation of hostilities-

If the minister would permit a question at this stage, does he argue that if the government decided not to issue the proclamation for two, three or four years, that delegation under the War Measures Act would be continued?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: No, I was just dealing with that very thing when the hon. member rose to put his question. I say that even now the extent covered by the delegation has already been diminished by reason of the changing situation which has occurred, and that has been recognized.

The situation is this. Under normal conditions there is a distribution of legislative powers by the British North America Act, and property and civil rights are within the exclusive jurisdiction of the provincial legislatures. But it has been decided that when a state of war arises property and civil rights have to be dealt with under other than their normal aspects; they have to be dealt with in the interests of the security and safety of the state as a whole; and because of that, the ordinary jurisdiction of parliament is enlarged. Parliament at no time can delegate more than it has. When it has, because of a state of war, a wider jurisdiction than it has normally, and it delegates all its powers, it delegates more than it could delegate in normal times. An act such as the War Measures Act could, if it were thought desirable to do so, be passed at any time. I do not think there has been a parliament since confederation that has not delegated some legislative function to the governor in council. The right to delegate does not depend upon the existence or nonexistence of war. What depends on the existence or non-existence of war is the enlarged jurisdiction that parliament can exercise during war. '
The hon. gentleman has asked whether if a government chose to delay issuing the proclamation, would it continuously be empowered to exercise by order in council the whole of the powers of parliament with the possible exception of taxation and the appropriation of money, because the supreme court in a case which went before it said it was not deciding whether that had been or could be delegated because of the terms of sections 53 and 54 of the British North America Act? But if a government chose to do a thing of that kind it would not be proceeding within the spirit of the War Measures Act.

What recourse
would a person have?
Mr. ST. LAURENT:	A member of parliament would have recourse by introducing at any time a bill to repeal the War Measures Act. The government is a committee of members of parliament, exercising powers because of the confidence placed in them by a majority in the House of Commons, and with no other right to do anything but the one that is based upon that fact.
I was not present when this statute was drafted. My impression on reading it is that the terms of section 2 were put there, not because it was felt that the powers would be abused, but because it was felt that there would have to be a definite starting point and a definite terminating date and that a gov-47696-44
ernment responsible to the House of Commons would properly comply with what would be supposed to be the desires of 'parliament and would make the proclamation at the proper time.

There were only
450 orders in council issued under the War Measures Act in the last war.
Mr. ST. LAURENT:	If the hon. member
will wait, I will give the exact number of orders in council that have been passed.

Under the War
Measures Act?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Not necessarily under the War Measures Act, because government has to be by order in council. I think I had better give the figures right away.
From September 1, 1939, up to September 28, 1945, the number of orders in council, including minutes of council, approved by the governor in council, totalled 58,402. During the same period the number of treasury board minutes passed was 36,329. Therefore the total number of formal acts of the governor in council during this period is 94,731.
Treasury board minutes deal almost entirely with appointments, resignations and other personnel matters in the civil service; with payments to firms and persons for services rendered; with remissions of taxes and the like. They represent approximately thirty-six to thirty-seven per cent of the total number of lets by the governor in council.
The total also includes minutes of council passed under the Munitions and Supply Act, authorizing contracts for the supply of goods or services necessary for the prosecution of the war. This group represents forty to forty-five per cent of the total.
About sixteen per cent consists of orders in council and minutes of council authorizing contracts for accommodation, supplies and services for government departments, appointments to senior positions in the public service and other instruments of a purely administrative nature and of no general interest.
The remaining two to three per cent which are of public interest is composed of regulations such as national selective service regulations, wartime prices and trade board regulations, and the defence of Canada regulations and other war-time legislation.
That is the situation. In this country and under our system of government we do by minutes of the treasury board, which are then submitted to the council and get their authority from the approval of the governor on the recommendation of council, and by orders in council, things which under a system like that of our neighbours to the south are

done by executive acts. A great many of these are purely formal. All these munitions and supply matters, if they involved a sum of more than a stated amount, had to be authorized by an order in council.

Would the minister permit a question: how many of these orders in council were passed under the provisions of the War Measures Act? I will elucidate that. In the last war the number was 450. Is it not a fact that the number under the War Measures Act during the period of this war is some eight or nine thousand?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I do not know. I have not had a calculation made, and I do not think it would be possible to make an accurate calculation. Mr. GEORGE BLACK (Yukon) moved the second reading of bill No. 2, to amend the Divorce Jurisdiction Act, 1930.
He said: In moving the second reading of this bill I do not know that I can make it any clearer to the house or put it in any better way than to read the explanatory note. It is sought to amend section 2 of the act which reads as follows:
A married woman who either before or after the passing of this act has been deserted by and has been living separate and apart from her husband for a period of two years and upwards and is still living separate and apart from her husband may, in any one of those provinces of Canada in which there is a court having jurisdiction to grant a divorce a vinculo matrimonii, commence in the court of such province having such jurisdiction proceedings for a divorce a vinculo matrimonii praying that her marriage may be dissolved on any grounds that may entitle her to such divorce according to the law of such province, and such court shall have jurisdiction to grant such divorce provided that immediately prior to such desertion the husband of such married woman was domiciled in the province in which such proceedings are commenced.
That last sentence is the unfair part of the act sought to be amended. The explanatory note states:
The purpose of this amendment is to vest jurisdiction in the divorce courts of the several provinces to try actions for divorce at the suit of a married woman deserted by and living apart from her husband where the woman has been residing in the province for not less than two years prior to the date of the commencement of such action.
As the law presently stands the woman may bring suit only in the province where the husband was domiciled immediately prior to the desertion. This condition of the law works a
47696-44i
great hardship on the deserted married woman who by reason of such desertion may have been forced to move to another province from that where the desertion took place. It is unreasonable that she should have to take her action back to the former.
Let me illustrate. Suppose a woman resident and living in British Columbia is married to a man who comes from Ontario to marry her, takes her back to Ontario and there deserts her. She by force of circumstances must go back to her old home in British Columbia because she no longer has support and maintenance from her husband, he having deserted her. She remains living in British Columbia and has the necessary material or evidence upon which, in ordinary circumstances, to apply for and get a divorce from a court having jurisdiction in such matters.
The provision of the bill as proposed is that if the woman lives for two years in the province to which she has returned, after the desertion of her husband, she may commence her action for divorce in that province. For instance, in the example I have given she would not have to go back to Ontario to commence the action. That is what I ask the house to support.

speakeroldname: Mr. JOSEPH ALFRED DION (Lake St. John-Roberval) (Translation):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as this is my first speech in the house, I take the opportunity of offering you my warmest congratulations on your election to the high position to which you have been named. Now that I am aware of the fine intellect, of the sense of justice and fairness which you have displayed in carrying out your duties since the opening of the session, I have no doubt that you are eminently qualified to fill the post for which you were chosen and will prove a worthy successor to your illustrious forerunners.
I also wish to congratulate the deputy Speaker elected last Thursday. I am not nersonally acquainted with him, but judging from the praise showered on him from both sides of the house, I have no doubt he is fully equipped to preside over our debates. I am happy to tender him my most sincere congratulations.
With reference to bill No. 2 before the house, I must say that I am opposed to it for the following reasons: first of all, on legal grounds, then I object to it for social reasons and . finally on moral and religious considerations.
To deal first with my objection on legal grounds: as a matter of fact, if we read the amendment submitted to the Divorce Jurisdiction Act of 1930, we find that its object
Divorce

is the extension, to a considerable degree, of the latitude granted those who wish to divorce in Canada.
First, let me quote the act as it is now. It reads as follows:
2. A married woman who either before or after the passing of this act has been deserted by and has been living separate and apart from her husband for a period of two years and upwards and is still living separate and apart from her husband may, in any one of those provinces of Canada in which there is a court having jurisdiction to grant a divorce a vinculo matrimonii, commence in the court of such province having such jurisdiction proceedings for a divorce a vinculo matrimonii praying that her marriage may be dissolved on any grounds that may entitle her to such divorce according to the law of such province, and such court shall have jurisdiction to grant such divorce provided that immediately prior to such desertion the husband of such married woman was domiciled in the province in which such proceedings are commenced.
It is intended to amend this section 2 and here is the text of the proposed amendment:
2. The court of any province of Canada vested with jurisdiction to grant a divorce a vinculo matrimonii shall have jurisdiction to entertain and try an action or other proceeding for divorce a vinculo matrimonii at the suit of a married woman who has resided in such province separate and apart from her husband for not less than two years immediately preceding the date of the commencement of such action or proceeding and on any grounds of entitlement to such divorce provided by the law of the province in which such court is constituted: Provided that she either was before or has been after the passing of this act deserted by and living separate and apart from her husband for a continuous period of not less than two years prior to the date of the commencement of such action or proceeding.
Briefly it means that a woman who has been domiciled with her husband in one of the provinces and who wishes to obtain a divorce merely has to live in another province, for two years to be entitled to apply for a divorce before a court of that province. In regard to the province of Quebec, where there are no divorce courts, a woman from that province might leave her husband, proceed across the boundary line into Ontario, a few miles from the province of Quebec, live there for two years and at the end of this period institute divorce proceedings against her husband in an Ontario court. In other words, this would enable married persons from the province of Quebec, where there are no divorce courts at present, to obtain a divorce in another province. This is my first legal ground against the proposed amendment. We *certainly cannot, in this indirect fashion, allow the people of Quebec, where no divorce *courts exist, to seek divorce in another province simply by living there for a period of

two years, sometimes by common consent of the parties concerned, as is often the case in divorce suits, when there is collusion.
Another reason for my opposition to this amendment is that it concerns the question of domicile which falls under civil rights. Under the British North America Act, the province has exclusive jurisdiction in matters of domicile, it is a field of provincial legislation. In the province of Quebec, this question is dealt with in the provincial civil code. However, the amendment before the house would transfer to another province the domicile of the person seeking divorce. A married woman would only have to go to any province, elect domicile there for a period of two years, and she would then be entitled to take a divorce action against her husband. I claim that a federal measure cannot deal with the question of domicile which is exclusively a provincial field of legislation and that even were parliament to pass this bill, it would be ultra vires, because it would then be legislating on a matter out of its jurisdiction. In the province of Quebec the domicile of a married woman is where her husband has his domicile.
I am opposing this bill from a legal standpoint on two grounds. The first is that it indirectly makes divorce possible for the people in the province of Quebec, there they cannot obtain it before their own courts. The second one is that this involves the question of domicile, a matter which lies solely within the purview of the civil law of each province.
Another ground on which I oppose this bill is that it evidently aims at facilitating divorce, which is a social evil. It may be a necessary evil in some cases, but it is nevertheless an evil, and every evil must be curbed as much as possible but never encouraged. Divorce, as every one knows, entails as a main consequence the disruption of the family. From a social standpoint the family is certainly the backbone of society. The family is what ensures continuity to the individual, and provides for him a link with the past and the future. An outstanding French orator, Jaures, has said that the individual is tied to life by the immutability of the tomb and by. the rocking of the cradles, in other words, by his ascendants and his descendants. Divorce, or the separation of married people, gives the custody of the children to one party or the other, thus destroying the social unit and jeopardizing the very existence of society. It is certainly tire worst evil of modem times.

Divorce
I feel we are right in stating that we should object to all legislation which tends to make divorce easier, more acceptable or more defensible.
I know we will be told there are many wretched, couples, especially since the great war when they met and married to live unhappily afterwards because of incompatibility. But must we, for that reason, intensify the evil by making divorce still more easily obtainable, which would increase the number of ill-assorted matches? That means that in five or ten years, even more people will be seeking divorce. Such a method of procedure, far from curbing the evil, is sure to spread it. Therefore, I believe we should oppose all measures which tend to facilitate the granting of divorce in our country.
As a last consideration, divorce, by setting itself against the indissoluble character of marriage is legislation of a purely pagan conception. I submit, therefore, that even if our country has no official religion, we are, nevertheless, a Christian nation. We are not ashamed to state it and I heard it proclaimed this afternoon. Further, daily, at the opening of the sitting, we invoke the Almighty and we express our faith in Christ. When peace was declared the leader of our nation did not hesitate to thank God, to make a confession of faith. If we are a Christian nation, if we abide by principles which distinguish us from pagan peoples, we must of necessity endeavour to prevent the adoption in our country of legislation tending to lead us back to paganism of olden times. History tells us that during the decline of ancient Rome, morals militated against the family and divorce was provided for in the laws. A woman no longer reckoned her age by the number of consuls but by the number of men she had married. Most assuredly, as divorce is made easier to obtain, the morals will become more dissolute and family life which is tire backbone of society will be jeopardized to a greater extent.
For all these reasons I object to the proposed amendment: first, from a legal standpoint, it is proposed by indirect means to enable married persons in tne provinces where there are no divorce courts to look elsewhere for such courts.
Second, because it involves the question of domicile, a matter which lies solely within the purview of provincial legislatures and because the proposed amendment would be unconstitutional if it were to be passed.
Finally, the third ground, as I said a few moments ago, is that a legislation tending to facilitate divorce would tend to disrupt society in weakening family ties. That is why, having
at heart the welfare of my country, I suggest that we should reject this amendment, holding on to the present provisions of the act so that we may ensure the happiness of the nation and the prosperity of the people.

(Text) Mr. Speaker, I consider it is my duty to say a few words about this measure. What is the purpose of this amendment? First, it is to facilitate the granting of divorces; second, to create a new jurisdiction for the granting of divorces; third, to oust the jurisdiction of our Quebec civil courts; fourth, to protect private interests to the prejudice of public interests, and fifth, to disorganize the family and society. The effect of the present amendment certainly would be prejudicial to the whole community. The rights of the husband are not protected. On what grounds can he base his defence if he is summoned to appear before a court in another province? It will be impossible for him to subpoena his witnesses. In many cases the wife will allege that her husband has abandoned her. If on the contrary the wife has abandoned her husband, the latter should have the right to prove the facts in support of his defence. Moreover, it would be conducive to serious abuses. The wife would have only to go abroad for four or five years, and then institute an action against her husband. If the common home were in Vancouver, the wife could take her action in Halifax. This would be a great distance from the Vancouver home, and would entail great expense if the husband wished to subpoena his witnesses and appear before the Halifax court.
Ab a matter of principle, a British subject has the right to be summoned before the court having jurisdiction in the place of his domicile, and there does not seem to be any serious reason for violating that rule. I contend, too, that this measure would disregard family rights. While a mother was abroad, the children might live with their father for some years. No matter what her behaviour might have been, she would have the right .to take proceedings against her husband, who has kept, the children. Social rights would be ini jeopardy. Any measure which facilitates; divorce divides the family, destroys the father's; and mother's authority, and ruins the children's; love.
(Translation) Mr. Speaker, I wish to sum-up my arguments as briefly as possible and' with my colleague, the hon. member for Lake St. John-Roberval (Mr. Dion), I invoke- the main reasons for my opposition to this amendment.
Divorce

The husband and wife must surely enjoy identical rights in connection -with divorce. It cannot be presumed in advance that the husband is in the wrong and the wife in the right or vice versa.
Then, if they enjoy the same right, why presume, in the present amendment, that the husband is in the wrong, by allowing the wife to take action against him in any province of Canada, be it far removed from the home she previously inhabited in the company of her husband? I claim that the object of this provision is purely and solely to facilitate the granting of divorces in this country. There is no other reason, for if a wife be deserted by her husband, if she be forsaken, as it is claimed, if she be deserving of the sympathy of the house and the whole country, it is evident that she will take action in the very place where she can secure witnesses, where her neighbours may give evidence in her favour. She will not seek, at a distance of 200 miles from her home, the protection of an unknown tribunal. It is so clearly evident that it would be pointless to formulate further arguments on the matter.
Moreover, as I said at the outset, the other party, the husband, is thereby denied the opportunity or even the possibility of bringing his witnesses before the court. Were this amendment to be passed, any wife could desert her husband, travel all over the country and after a few years, the husband having then given up all hope of rebuilding his home, she could take legal proceedings against him in some place where he would be unable to send his witnesses, and where it would perhaps be impossible for him to appear before the said court. Therefore, he would be unable to enter a defence plea and he would then lose by default, which would mean the wangling by indirect means, of a divorce that could not have been obtained from a court sitting at the place of residence of both parties.
Mr. Speaker, to all intents and purposes, this brings into being a new jurisdiction. There are the jurisdiction ratione materiae and the jurisdiction ratione [DOT]personae.. It is an absolute 'right, recognized as well in the province of Quebec as in the others, that a person should be tried before the court of his domicile, and it is one of those rights which is most treasured by a citizen.
Mr. Speaker, I realize that the jurisdiction ratione personae must be respected and cannot be set aside by such an amendment.
Indeed, it is a very subtle amendment. It is said: this poor woman who has been deserted by her husband, why force her to incur expenses and compel her to return to the domicile where she lived with him? Let us

allow her to go somewhere else and she will merely apjfly for divorce in the court of her choice. Well, Mr. Speaker, this goes very far, inasmuch as to-day in the province of Quebec we have no divorce court, we have safeguarded this principle, thank God. Thanks to the efforts of our predecessors in this house civil courts determine the rights of the parties. Under this amendment, the women of the province of Quebec could go to another province where a divorce court has been set up, live there for at least two years and then institute proceedings and obtain a divorce which they could not obtain in the province of Quebec. Further, this would result in granting new jurisdiction to a court of another province, a jurisdiction which it did not have over a person from the province of Quebec and to which in our opinion it is not entitled over persons under the jurisdiction of the province of Quebec.
Besides, and this follows from what I have just said, our courts would be deprived of their jurisdiction, they would be prevented from dispensing civil law in our province. In Quebec it is provided that the husband or the wife may appear before the court of their place of domicile, where in many cases conjugal disputes are settled amicably and family life continues.
If we agreed to this amendment, we would encourage divorce and prevent our courts from exerting the beneficent influence they have wielded in the past. Moreover, this legislation affects private interests, rather than general interest and public order and I believe that in such a matter public interest must be the first consideration. This amendment, whose purpose is to enhance a private interest, tends to facilitate the application of the divorce law which, in my opinion, cannot be accepted in a Christian and well ordered society.
Divorce divides the family. It obviously dissociates husband and wife who will thereafter live apart. Moreover, the children must be considered; they are parted from father or mother and, when remarriage follows with its , consequent offspring, we behold incongruous multiple paternities, a state of things which should not exist in a Christian society.
I will go even further, Mr. Speaker, and contend that divorce also disorganizes the community. Family life is at the core of our Canadian society. No distinction is made between races, religious beliefs or other opinions. Here, in Canada, our community life is still based on the family unit which remains the cornerstone of our national structure.

Hear, hear.

Divorce

We still count on the
family to ensure the survival of our Christian society, and our Canadian citizens, whatever their religious belief, are devoted to their family and want this social cell maintained in Canada. If we were to let divorce become easier to obtain family ties would become disrupted, paternal authority would be undermined and children would lose that love for their parents which the latter have instilled into them, and this would lead us inevitably and in a short time to atheism.
Mr. Speaker, sublime thoughts have been expressed in this house following the end of hostilities. Several members on both sides of the house have suffered personal losses; several have lost their sons, their relatives in battle. Why? To fight the forces of evil and to defend righteousness.
Right has emerged triumphant in this six-year struggle which unleashed the powers of evil against those of decency, and we may now look forward to an era of freedom and prosperity.
The forces of decency are vested in the family, they are based on love while those of evil are inspired by hatred. The ideology of our enemies rested on hatred while our own was founded on love.
We oppose divorce and roundabout means of promoting it because we favour a Christian society based on the principles of charity and love. If we want the forces of decency to develop, consolidate and flourish in our country, let us set aside this subtle little amendment which some want to insert in our laws. It is a trap which will end by allowing all Canadian citizens straightway to obtain a divorce wherever they may be. I feel convinced that even in provinces where divorce is recognized and where divorce courts are found, all well thinking people regret the existence of such anomalous conditions in our social legislation. I am sure the amendment will come to its natural end and it will not be necessary to add another chapter to this unfortunate legislation.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I wish to point out that I am concerned merely with the future of my fellow-citizens, those of my own race and of others as well.
(As a Canadian citizen, I yearn to see, all over the country, strong united families, where education, under the wise leadership of father and mother who are in full accord is directed to the thorough development of every potentiality and eveiy talent. Let these families remain united, yielding to the full extent of their powers, flourish, in a regulated order and we shall then enjoy liberty and happiness in our country.
(Text) Mr. ELPHEGE MARIER (Jacques-
Cartier): Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words about this amendment to the Divorce Jurisdiction Act, 1930. The bill as presented seems very simple, but in my opinion it has some far-reaching consequences. The hon. member for Lake St. John-Roberval (Mr. Dion) has already dealt with the legal rights of the province of Quebec. If my information is correct, I understand that there are only two provinces in Canada without divorce courts, Quebec and Prince Edward Island. If this bill is passed the province of Quebec will be affected. A wife will be permitted to go to Ontario, reside there for two years, then apply to the courts of Ontario for a divorce and in that way escape the jurisdiction of the courts of Quebec the court of her domicile. At the same time her husband would not be given the same privilege.
I am against divorce on religious grounds and because of the evils, both moral and material, that spring from divorce. I do not intend to discuss this bill from that angle, but I do insist that it would be against the civil rights of the provinces. I should like to refer to section 92 of the British North America Act which determines the exclusive powers of the provinces.
(Translation): I shall quote three paragraphs of section 92 of the British North America Act which is entitled: "Exclusive powers of provincial legislatures":
12.	The solemnization of marriage in the province;
13.	Property and civil rights in the province.
14.	The administration of justice in the province, including the constitution, maintenance and organization of provincial courts.
Therefore, under the provisions of sub-section 14 of section 92 of the British North America Act, the province alone has the right to set up divorce courts. And in our province, it has not been deemed advisable so far to create such courts. If our province did not deem advisable to set up such courts, I do not see why a roundabout way would be resorted to in order to give certain citizens of the province the right to evade the jurisdiction of the court of their province by availing themselves of the rights and privileges granted in a neighbouring province. And this is exactly what would take place if the wife could avail herself of the court of a neighbouring province in order to exercise rights which her own province deny them.
In sub-section 12 of the British North America Act, reference is made to the solemnization of marriage. I have always understood that this paragraph reserves to the provinces the right to legislate on such solem-
Divorce

nization as well as to determine the rights of the husband and wife arising from such marriage. This is the reason why there are in the province of Quebec as well as in the other provinces certain laws which control the solemnization of marriage and its consequences. Here again, the proposed amendment would tend to destroy or modify the laws or the obligations which arise from the solemnization of marriage.
Now, sub-section 13, which grants exclusive powers to the provinces concerning property and civil rights in the province would be set aside by the proposed amendment. Indeed, the civil rights of the provinces include right over persons and right over property. To my mind, the right over persons would disappear or rather would be curtailed if a person domiciled in the province of Quebec could get away and after residing two years in another province, could obtain a divorce under conditions and according to laws which are different from those of the province where she is domiciled. Especially in the province of Quebec, the law which establishes the domicile of the wife at her husband's residence would be violated. And not only the law regarding domicile would be violated but also numerous other rights arising from marriage. In obtaining a divorce either in Ontario or in New-Brunswick or in Nova Scotia or in any other province, there would also be another disadvantage for the parties concerned for the court granting the divorce could not affect the rights arising from marriage or the obligations pertaining thereto. Indeed, in our province, the question of joint estate, which does not occur in other provinces, must be taken into account. Therefore, a court of another province could not, in granting a divorce, determine the respective rights of the interested parties and as, in Quebec, divorce is not recognized, they might find themselves in an embarrassing position. After securing a divorce in another province, a person enjoying certain rights in the common estate, would lose her rights on account of the change in its status, because the common estate is not recognized in this other province.
The same principle would apply to gifts and privileges often resulting from marriage and which exist also in other provinces. If the court granting divorce is unable to grant the civil rights enjoyed by the interested parties the clauses included in the marriage contract could not be taken into consideration on account of the divorce granted, because the said court could not deal, in its findings, with the assets of the consorts and furthermore,

no court of our province could settle the matter, as divorce is not recognized within its borders.
There is also the status of children. Sometimes, the marriage contract provides that children to be born will be entitled to certain gifts which could not be realized at the time of divorce because, I repeat, the province of Quebec would not recognize the divorce.
But the province of Quebec is not the only one concerned in this matter; in other provinces there are also numerous legislative measures relating to the assets of the consorts in case of separation or annulment of marriage. Several provinces, as I said, would be in the same position when having to determine the rights of spouses.
I need not elaborate further on the anomalous situation that would be created by an unconstitutional law. If the privilege of establishing civil rights belongs exclusively to the provinces, as it is clearly stated in section 92, I do not see how, through an amendment to the divorce act, an individual could be allowed to evade the laws of his province, provided he lived somewhere else for a certain period, while as a matter of fact his true domicile was there.
Therefore, from a constitutional standpoint, the bill should not become law. From the standpoint of provincial rights, and of the consequences which the passing of this amendment might entail in our province, it should not be enacted.
The time when we hear so much about union and brotherhood, speak of organizing to solve so many complex problems with which we are faced, to my mind, I say, such a time is ill-chosen for raising a question as important as that of divorce. A matter of this order might stir up animosity between certain provinces or sections of the country. We should not raise such an issue but instead tend to the serious problems submitted to our attention and which are far more essential to the future of our country that this amendment to the existing divorce legislation whose purpose is to render the decree more easily obtainable and is in the sole interest of a few people under particular circumstances. If there were no other means of redress I would agree that some amendment was needed to provide for the plan mentioned a ^hort while ago by my hon. colleague. The required means, however, are already in existence and will adequately take care of the few exceptional cases in our province where no divorce court is found. I am therefore opposed to this amendment and hope it will be defeated.

(Translation) Mr. Speaker, to indicate my opposition to the bill under consideration, I wish to add a few remarks to those already so brilliantly made by my colleague.
We, from Quebec, believe that the ties of marriage can only be broken by the natural death of the consorts. As long as both live, marriage remains indissoluble. Such is the fundamental principle enunciated in section 185 of the province of Quebec Civil Code. We, of Quebec, believe that the indissolubility of marriage is at the very foundation of the family, which, as was stated a few minutes ago, is the primary cell of society.
As Christians, we, of Quebec, believe that divorce is opposed to divine law and, as Canadians, we claim that it is in contradiction with natural law, in this sense that the indissolubility of marriage is directly connected with the best interests of society.
The real object of marriage is not only the raising of future generations, but also the protection and education of children.
For this reason, Mr. Speaker, I claim that we should find among the most indomitable enemies of divorce all those who profess to be Christians, all those who think in terms of society, all those who have at heart the lofty interests of the Canadian nation.
If we refer to the figures published in connection with divorce in Canada, we are appalled to realize to what an abyss we are sinking. And we understand that the time has come to alter our course in the right direction, to pull ourselves together, and the only way to accomplish this is to make it harder to obtain a divorce in our country.
In 1901 th'ere were only 661 divorces in Canada, for a population of 5,300,000; in 1911, 1,530 actions were taken and in 1921, the number had climbed to 7,401. Between 1911 and 1921, a period similar to the present one, inasmuch as it was marked by an armed conflict, the troublous times resulted in a five-fold increase in the number of divorces, which climbed from 1,500 to 7,401. In 1941, divorces numbered 14,032 in our country compared to 7,441 in 1931. This is an increase of practically 100 per cent. On the strength of these figures, unless we endeavour to curb this tendency, if the five-fold increase in the number of divorces holds for the period 1941 to 1951 as for that of 1911 to 1921, 70.000 homes will have been broken in Canada in the ten years previous to 1951.
Mr. Speaker, divorce is a national curse; in fact, it is national suicide. To-day every country in the wortd realizes how much divorce decreases the birth-rate and to what extent it constitutes not only a factor of family
disruption and social disorganization, but also a threat of extinction for the population of some countries. Quite recently, on September 27, the British government stated that the numerical strength and even the survival of the British nation were endangered by the increase in the number of divorces and by birth-control. In that white book, published in conformity with a procedure reserved for official statements of major importance, it is explicitly said that there is an ultimate danger, quite real although remote, that the British people may gradually disappear-and that statement is made by the British government itself. That blue book emphasizes that in 1919, for instance, Great Britain had about
16.000.	000 people under the age of twenty, while in 1939, twenty years after, she had only
14.000.	000. So much for England.
Let us see what happens to-day in godless Soviet Russia. In 1943, the government of Soviet Russia discarded the communist principle of coeducation and reestablished separate schools for boys and girls. Last year-I quote from an article published on July 10 by the newspaper Le Droit of Ottawa-the soviet government itself announced that they-
-had just taken new measures with a view to ensuring the morality and the survival of the Russian family, threatened in its very existence by the devastation of war and by the ravages, no less serious, of the anti-family policy forced upon the Russians during twenty-five years of communist administration.
I quote further:
The Soviet authorities make divorce more difficult to obtain.
If Russia has come to realize that after twenty-five years of communism she must make divorce more difficult to obtain it is high time that we should realize it in Canada. Again:
Russian couples only had to sign a form and appear for a few minutes before an official in order to obtain the dissolution of their marriage.
That is what we do not want in Canada. It is why I oppose the bill of the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Black). Let me quote in conclusion, a most eloquent excerpt from a paper read by Mr. Leon Mercier-Gouin, now a member of the Senate, before a social congress held in Montreal in 1923. Here are a few lines which will certainly not fail to impress you:
Divorce is a demoralizing factor and it further checks the birth rate.
If there are children, divorce deprives them of the care and moral education they have a right to expect from their parents, for the latter have irrevocably separated and perhaps remarried. Thus the unwanted child is unnaturally divided between father and mother. Separation as to bed and board is a sad evil, sometimes necessary; it is a cruel hardship for
War and Demobilization

a child, but not an iniquitous injustice lacking all possibility of readjustment. Divorce does grievous wrong to tiny tots who did not ask to be born. Their young hearts are withered by this blot which, like cancer, gnaws at their conscience and sensibilities. Divorce destroys the family and thus shatters at its very base the whole social structure.
I maintain that divorce is anti everything that matters: family, society, legislation, contractual obligations, Christianity and nationhood. That is why we oppose it irrevocably.

the hon. member, but as the time allotted for the discussion of government measures has expired, the house must resume where it left off at six o'clock.

Our committee has also given additional consideration to some of the topics of the main report, and we wish to submit the following for attention:
1.	Continuation of controls after the war. There appear to be many who believe that some measure of control, specially in relation to ceiling prices, should be had and continued for some time after the war as a transit and adjustment period policy. Otherwise prices might jump suddenly to extreme limits, and bring a chaotic situation.
2.	Should the necessary controls be continued under the War Measures Act?
It is expected by some, feared by others, that the federal government, for such controls as may appear necessary to maintain, will continue to rely on the authority of the War Measures Act.
Now that the war is over, such a course would raise a very serious problem of constitutional law, as to controlling civil and property rights which. are in relation to civil law, and fall normally, under the constitution within the exclusive legislative jurisdiction of the provinces.
Authorities are cited to show that it is well established that circumstances, very serious in nature, and amounting to a national emergency, such as a great war or other similarly wide and calamitous circumstances, would justify the federal power, by legislation, adequately to control the liberties, civil rights and property in the provinces.
We then come to the recommendations which are as follows:
Your committee recommend that the proclamation declaring that the war no longer exists be issued as soon as the war with the enemy is really at an end according to the established principles of international law.
Let us make the distinction here between the war emergency itself, which is the fact of a state of war, and an economic emergency, which, though a consequence following the war, is not the war emergency. It may be an economic emergency. The calamity against which we have to protect the nation is not the war itself, or a consequential defeat of our arms, or the invasion by the enemy, but is an economic state of affairs that may be most serious, and that may, or may not be adequately coped with by the provinces. If the federal administration feel that, after the war, and in relation to such economic conditions of the country, a state of emergency exists, of a most serious character, and national in scope, let them face the issue directly and submit to parliament a new law affirming the existence or the apprehension and determining the exact nature of the new emergency.

speechtext:
Hear, hear.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I appreciate the "hear, hear" from the other side of the house. As a

War and Demobilization
matter of fact, the speech from the throne had been drafted before anything of this became public, and if the hon. members will refer to it as printed on page 8 of Hansard they will find the following:
It is the intention of the government to abolish war restrictions in progressive steps as rapidly as that can be accomplished without occasioning inflation or other economic disturbances. Such controls as are essential to the welfare of our people will be continued for as long as they are necessary.
You will be asked to approve a measure to extend certain specified emergency powers to meet emergency conditions in the period of reconstruction.
As a matter of fact, I have before me a bill with that intent, which was printed evidently before August 28, because the stamp from my office bears the date of August 28, and just as soon as there is an opportunity that bill will be introduced and parliament will be asked to take its responsibility, because it will be a considerable responsibility. It would be a considerable responsibility for anyone to take to sweep out with one fell stroke those controls which have been so effective in preventing inflation in this country. In making that statement I am not departing from principles which were enunciated by the leader of the Progressive Conservative party in a speech he made in Montreal on April 23, 1945, in which he said this:
In thus referring to our war-time controls I do not suggest that these have been bad, or that they were an unnecessary product of autocratic power. Their necessity must be as clear to you as it is to me; but I insist that in assessing their virtues we should think of those controls in terms of the job they were intended to do. If we do that, then I am sure you will not find it contradictory for me to say that existing controls cannot be dropped willy-nilly the instant the job of making war is done. Certainly we must be rid of them as soon as possible, but in some cases they will have to be unwound very carefully and slowly and there will have to be planning to accomplish the unwinding.
That is not my language; that is the opinion of the leader of the opposition; and we find ourselves in company with the privy council in the Fort Frances case in which the following is stated at page 706 of the report.
No authority other than the central government is in a position to deal with a problem which is essentially one of statesmanship. It may be that it has become clear that the crisis which arose is wholly at an end, and that there is no justification for the continued exercise of an exceptional interference which becomes ultra vires when it is no longer called for. In such a case the law as laid down for distribution of powers in the ruling instrument would have to be invoked.
The question of determining at what time it will be proper to put an end to the validity of orders made under the War Measures Act is a matter of statesmanship. We do not pretend that we are the only statesmen in this house. The intention of the government, as stated in the speech from the throne, is to ask all the statesmen in this house to take their responsibility as to the proper time for putting an end to these controls. The matter will be gone into quite fully when the bill comes before the house.
I do not want to take the time at this moment when we are dealing with an appropriation of money that is necessary for purposes directly connected with the war, to discuss the reasons for the continuation of controls which will have to be discussed when the bill announced in the speech from the throne comes properly before the house for consideration; but I would refer hon. members to the reference book on economic controls which was put before the members of the dominion-provincial conference. Once again this is a matter where emergency conditions enlarge the powers of the dominion at the expense of those normally exercised by provincial authorities. The reasons given or suggested for it being necessary to continue that state of the legislation for a time were summarized in this reference book compiled under the direction of the committee on economic controls, of which F. P. Varcoe was chairman and C. Stein, secretary. This book contains submissions from the wartime prices and trade board, the war industries control board and the Department of Labour. The purpose of this material is-
. . . to describe the situation which brought various war-time economic controls into being and to outline the kind of problems which probably will continue to exist in these fields during the transition period.
This summary contains some thirty pages of double column print, to show why some, thinking they were taking the position of statesmen, suggested that careful consideration ought to be given to the possible consequences of too rapidly proceeding with decontrol. The policy the government of Canada submitted to the representatives of the governments of the provinces in that regard is set out on page 9 of the proposals of the government of Canada, which were put before that conference. There hon. members will find a long statement of the methods which the dominion government proposed as being best suited to the progressive elimination of these controls.
Another question which was put and which quite logically follows this portion of my remarks is: have the defence of Canada regula-
War and Demobilization

tiona been repealed? Practically all the defence of Canada regulations which were of substance have been repealed by two orders in council which were published in the war orders and regulations. One was passed on August 16, the day after we heard of the intention of the Japanese government to surrender to the allied powers, and it did away with practically all those provisions of the defence of Canada regulations which interfered with the ordinary liberties of the individuals. The second was passed on September 14, 1945, and was published in the September 24 issue of war orders and regulations. It removed many of the other regulations, leaving subsisting practically only those dealing with protected places or areas, which were necessary because of very important works going on, as for instance at Chalk river, in plants belonging to the government. Other provisions were retained because of our international obligations with respect to the control of tonnage, and the provisions which give special authority for the placing of ships in harbours were also retained. It was felt necessary to retain those provisions for the safety of the men being brought back from overseas. They were passed subsequently to the list of orders in council which were tabled by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) at the opening of the session, which brought the tabling down to June 30, and I would ask leave to table those orders in council now.
Another question which arose and about which I am sure there is much unsatisfied curiosity in my own mind as well as in the minds of others is the date which will be fixed as that from which will run the two years for the refunding of the compulsory savings portion of the income tax, and the refundable portion of the excess profits tax. My understanding is that this date will be announced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) in presenting his budget proposals. Likewise many of the previous controls which were found to be no longer absolutely necessary have been eliminated.
Is there anyone in this house who would have taken the responsibility, either on August 15 or on August 16, or on September 1 or on September 2, of saying the war was at an end, and that everything in our system of controls on which we depended to combat inflation would then come to an end? I do not think a single member of this house would have said at that time, or would say at this time, that it was proper to bring that system down without taking some means to substitute other authority for the maintenance of those controls. That is the manner in which the law officer has advised his colleagues; that
fMr. St. Laurent.]
is a matter the responsibility for which will be placed before this house as soon as it is possible to introduce and deal with the bill thus forecast in the speech from the throne.

Mr. Speaker, it would have been well if the minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent), who is also Attorney General of Canada, had given this opinion on September 11, the day I raised this question here. Notwithstanding that he read from some correspondence, it is a legal opinion. Ever since confederation it has been the rule in this parliament that the Minister of Justice, who is also Attorney General of Canada, should not give legal opinions in this house, even when he is asked for them. That question has come up on many occasions. The rule I mention has been followed since about 1886, and there are good reasons for it. In this country the courts are subservient to the legislature. One of the principles I have always enunciated is this. The Minister of Justice appoints the judges. One of the cardinal principles of our constitution is that we must have impartial justice and a judiciary free from any interference on the part of the executive. That has been the reason for the rule I just mentioned.
I brought this matter to the attention of the house on September 11 when, in reference to this resolution, in view of the fact that the war was over, I asked if the government did not consider that the War Measures Act had been automatically repealed and annulled, that it had expired through the effluxion of time; and I still believe that is the correct view. At that time I was not brushed aside, as some newspapers said. I am not in the habit of being treated in that way, because I know the facts of the case. At that time the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) replied to me:
It is the opinion of the Minister of Justice that it is within the constitutional power of this parliament to pass this bill. Moreover, this bill, as I say, follows the precedent of the Demobilization Appropriation Act passed in June of 1919.
This war is totally different from the last one. Such an act as that passed in 1919 is not relevant in the house at the present time. I call the attention of hon. members to the statements made by the Canadian Bar Association, where they have given some opinions which the Minister of Finance has said were only matters of policy. I say they were not They were legal opinions on the whole question
Let us follow this to its logical conclusion In view of what the Minister of Justice said to-night, the whole control system is still in effect, despite the fact that the war is over. The war may be over in London and over in

War and Demobilization
Washington, but apparently it is not over here. They have taken action in Washington in connection with their controls. They have loosened them up, and have given large and small businessmen a chance. Let us follow their example.
Sometimes these controls need rationing. If they are continued large numbers of people will be summoned to law courts across this dominion. We know that many summonses have been issued already, and chiefly in the Toronto district. The charges and fines there seem to be about ten to one, so far as numbers are concerned, when compared with what they are in other cities. There is no equality of treatment at all. When these cases are before the courts the question will be raised whether this parliament has power, in view of the war being over, and the War Measures Act annulled, to follow the practice which it has followed of bringing in resolutions of this kind, followed by bills.
I referred to this matter the night war broke out in September, 1939. I referred to the very same principle which is now involved, and which has been discussed this evening by the Minister of Justice. I pointed out that when Great Britain is at war, Canada is at war, and that when Great Britain is no longer at war, Canada is no longer at war.
Then, on the matter of status, I say we were not at war, although war was declared on September 3, 1939. However, it was not until September 10 of that year that this House of Commons enacted legislation. On September 4 the Athenia was sunk, and I called attention of the house to the fact that we were bound by what had been, done, and were at war on September 3, 1939. As a result of that we found out afterwards that under our new system of status we had to wait until September 10, for seven days, and all that kind of thing, before Canada declared war.
All I am saying is this, that no matter what we say or do in this house, this matter will come up in the law courts of the country. It will come before the courts the very moment it is proposed after the war to enforce these controls. The jurisdiction of parliament will be challenged, so far as its legislation in this respect is concerned.
Fines will be imposed and1 appeals will be lodged. In my view they should be taken right to the supreme court; that is where this matter should go. Under the Supreme Court Act the government of the day, on recommendation of the attorney general, can recommend submission to the Supreme Court of Canada of points such as those raised by me
on September 11 and a few days ago in the speech of the very able hon.. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker).
In view of what has been said to-night by the Minister of Justice, surely a clear case has been made out, if there ever was a case made out for reference to the supreme court under the Supreme Court Act. If ever there was such a case, it is this one now before us. The whole question of the system of controls as they are to be permitted in Canada after the war is over should be looked into.
I shall refer to one or two further points, and then I shall have concluded. My first point has to do with paragraphs (a), (b), (c), (d) and (e) of the resolution now before us. We have seen the result of our system of controls in Canada. As I said the other day:
All kinds of bodies, over the head of parliament, are spending money like water. Every principle for which the British nation struggled in the old land since the seventeenth century has been surrendered to the political caucuses. Parliament itself, which came into being to ensure that taxes shall be voted only by those who have to pay them, has become the institution through which those who do not pay them impose them on others.
I want to emphasize to the committee that powers of legislation older even than the right of taxpayers to determine the national expenditure have been surrendered, and if we are to continue this sort of thing the power of parliament will be gone forever. Whole spheres of activity, involving the livelihood of every man, woman and child in this country, have been removed from the jurisdiction of the law and of parliament and reserved for the determination of tribunals, irresponsible, irremovable, governed by no control and subject to no appeal.
That is all I object to. If parliament is to be supreme we should observe its rights and privileges. Before going into committee we are told by the various ministers about the succes sof this system of control. In addition to that, some controllers are going across Canada making speeches about which, quite probably, the ministers know nothing. This is done over the head of parliament and while it is in session.
There was some legislation passed after the last war, when parliament was meeting, to require the submission of all these matters to the House of Commons. This has not been done. In addition to that, I contended at the time this war started, during the first ten days of the special session, that we did not need any proclamation or order in council; that war was on from September 3, 1939. We did not need any orders in council such as were passed by parliament on September 10, 1939. We did not need them, because when Great Britain is at war, Canada is at war, and when she is not, Canada is not.
War and Demobilization

I know it is in the public interest to have the removal of these government controls. There is no business, large or small, in Canada that is not suffering from them. Large business, wholesale business, retail business-all kinds of business have been suffering from these irksome controls.
I should like to draw to the attention of the house what has been done in the United States, because throughout the war it would seem that we followed Washington to a considerable extent. This pamphlet sets out the policy of the federal government in that country, and the measures taken by federal agencies. This booklet, which is issued monthly by the National City bank of New York city, in its September issue sets out what is being done at Washington. This is the action taken by the President of the United States on the advice of his officers, and particularly Mr. Snyder, director of the office of war mobilization and reconversion. It also contains suggestions by Mr. Krug, chairman of the war production board. These men occupy positions which would be the equivalent of positions in our Department of Munitions and Supply.
Perhaps I might say in passing, and before reading from the report, that our parliament might well follow what has been done at Washington in connection with the elimination of these controls and in respect of reconversion. In other countries the test of the ability to recover from a war and to return to a state of prosperity has been found in the capacity to produce goods and to supply them to the population. There is no other measuring stick than that found in the ability to produce, distribute and consume goods and services. If production is insufficient, then the distribution of money, whether in the form of international loans or relief, would be involved. Many industries do not have to reconvert at all, and those that do make their preparations well in advance. Industrial leaders throughout the United States generally know what they are doing and what they are going to do. They are moving forward, in a sense of public responsibility, and because they see vast markets awaiting their products.
Returning to the report of the National City bank, I find this, with respect to the removal of government controls, in the report of Mr. Snyder, approved in August by President Truman:
Finally, and perhaps most important of all, the policies of the federal government and the measures taken by the federal agencies imply in general that reliance for rapid reconversion is being placed upon the ingenuity and resourcefulness of business men themselves, and not upon schemes for government direction and control. Nothing was more to be feared, either ['Mr. Church.]
for the transition period or the longer future, than regulations subjecting every major decision of business to the approval of Washington, with the certain result of confusion, delay, mistakes and injustices. But the moves since the surrender have shown that the policy is to free business of interferences with production 

in some respects at once and in others gradually

and put it on its own. The first step was to cancel war contracts promptly, in order to cut the cost and stop the waste of war, reduce the inflation danger, free materials, machines and labour for peace time goods, and clear the decks for a fresh start.
In a short paragraph, the policy of the director at Washington is set out, and this was reported to the president on August 15. It is as follows:
Nor will we continue the manufacture of useless armaments for as much as one day to c ishion the shock. We will not manufacture a single shell, nor a single piece of equipment above absolute minimum military needs, for the purpose of reducing the shock of terminating war work. We will not keep a single soldier or sailor in uniform longer than he is needed by the army or navy, in order to hold down the totals of temporary unemployment. This is the policy laid down by the congress, wholeheartedly carried out by this administration, and backed by the American people.
And again:
The second step was to remove most of the war-time limitations on production and on the use of materials. Mr. Krug, chairman of the war production board, has moved rapidly, rescinding limitation orders except in the case of certain critically short items, and in general freeing the industries to go ahead without having, as the Truman committe report in 1944 said, "to go to Washington with hat in hand."
This man occupies somewhat the same position as our Minister of Reconstruction (Mr. Howe), and this is what he said:
It is necessary to get rid of regulations and production limitations as quickly as possible. They^ automatically put ceilings on initiative, imagination and r'-esourcefulness, the very qualities the country will need most if we are to have a resilient and rapidly expanding economy after the defeat of Japan.
The danger confronting us, as I see it, is that we will overlook the natural resilience of the economy-the capacity of manufacturers, wholesalers and retailers to readapt themselves to changed conditions and hence quickly to utilize the resources released from munitions production. If we were to attempt in Washington to see that every manufacturer, wholesaler or retailer got his exact share of released manpower or materials, we should be lost in a myriad of rules and regulations. We should get in the way of reconversion rather than speed it. -
And again:
As long as the policies of government are in harmony with these principles, the energies, abilities and experience of millions of business men will be at work, each on his own problems, to get factories retooled and speed production of civilian goods. No other forces that could be exerted in the situation could possibly be as effective.

War and Demobilization
And again:
The allegation that there has been a "lack of planning" does not stand analysis. Probably there has never been a time when planning, at the level where it counts most, has been as widespread and as ably done.
And further down:
The overwhelming majority of the American people, however, believe that detailed regulation of business in peace time would be wholly impracticable and disastrous in its consequences upon production and employment.
If we are to avoid widespread unemployment the government must release some of these controls and leave large and small businesses free to carry on. I notice in the newspapers that estimates are being made of unemployment. One made by the president of the C.I.O. in the United States is as high as 10,000,000. The same predictions were made at the end of the last war. I notice it is estimated that there will be 500,000 unemployed in Canada. These are rot, and some restraint should prevent the circulation of such predictions. I believe, with the experience gained in the war, the reconversion of industry in Canada will be carried on more rapidly than was the case in the last war. If private business is allowed to function free of control, as is the case at Washington reconversion will be much shorter.
If there is to be any danger of the suffering which occurred in this country after the last war during the first winter occurring now that this war is over, the government should be ready to look after those who may suffer because of lack of shelter, food or fuel.
